"Those are some simple activities that you can do that will make huge changes in the future," the interim surgeon general added.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Man who beat rare cancer celebrates by canoeing 2,000 miles with his dog
summary: Frank Carter, 67, and his dog Amos completed a 2,000-mile canoe trip down the Missouri River four years after CAR T-cell therapy cleared his lymphoma.
story: Patient Laurie Adami credits the cancer treatment Car-T with saving her life on ‘Fox News @ Night.’

A 67-year-old cancer survivor from Orange County, Florida, completed a more than 2,000-mile journey down the Missouri River alongside his dog, Amos, after undergoing a groundbreaking immunotherapy treatment.
Frank Carter spent 64 days navigating the longest U.S. river in a cedar-strip canoe he built by hand, according to reports from the Moffitt Cancer Center and FOX 13 News.
The expedition began in Montana and concluded near St. Louis, Missouri, requiring the pair to camp along the riverbank while enduring severe storms, high winds and hail, FOX 13 News reported.
'FIT MOM' DID 'EVERYTHING RIGHT' — THEN A COLON CANCER DIAGNOSIS CHANGED HER LIFE

Before his diagnosis, Carter was a long-distance adventurer. According to the Moffitt Cancer Center, he spent five months hiking the Appalachian Trail in 2019 and completed an eight-week cross-country bicycle ride from San Diego to New Smyrna Beach, Florida, in 2020.
However, his physical limits were tested in a new way in 2021 after a routine 5K race.
Frank Carter, a 67-year-old cancer survivor from Orange County, Fla., paddled 2,341 miles down the Missouri River over 64 days with his golden retriever, Amos. (UCG/Universal Images Group via G)
"I was wiped out. I just wasn't recovering," Carter told FOX 13 News. "I went to my doctor, had blood tests. Long story short, in two weeks I was getting chemo."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Doctors diagnosed Carter with mantle cell lymphoma, a rare form of blood cancer that originates in white blood cells known as lymphocytes. He underwent 15 rounds of chemotherapy in Orlando, according to Moffitt Cancer Center.
Carter hand-built the cedar-strip canoe (not pictured) for the journey, and is now sharing his story to encourage other patients to remain active and hopeful. (iStock)
Although the treatment significantly reduced the cancer, follow-up exams showed lingering traces of the disease.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Carter then sought care at the Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa to undergo chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, which involves extracting the patient's own immune cells, genetically altering them in a laboratory to identify cancer cells, and adding them back into the body.
Doctors treated Carter with CAR T-cell therapy, a groundbreaking immunotherapy that genetically alters a patient's own T-cells to attack cancer, leaving him cancer-free for four years. (iStock)

"We take those T-cells and genetically engineer them by putting something called a CAR into them," Dr. Michael Jain, an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center, told FOX 13 News. "Now these T-cells can see the tumor and get rid of it, where before the tumor was able to hide from it."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Carter has remained cancer-free for four years after the single infusion. Throughout his recovery, he has found constant support in his dog, Amos, whom he brought home right before beginning chemotherapy.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"After my cancer diagnosis, I told myself I was going to beat this, and I really wanted a dog during the process," Carter told Moffitt's Endeavor publication. "I got Amos right before my first treatment."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Longer lives, worse health? Scientists uncover troubling trend across generations
summary: The morbidity gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy is widest in America, where people spend about 14 years in poor health.
story: Rates of chronic disease, obesity and stress continue to rise across America. Experts warn that some of the healthiest habits from the nation's earlier centuries may have fallen by the wayside.
People across the world are living longer, but they’re also spending more years coping with ill health, a recent study observed.

The "morbidity gap" — the number of years people spend in poor health, typically struggling with chronic challenges such as low back pain, hearing loss and depression — widened across 203 of 204 countries analyzed and was the most pronounced in America, the researchers found.

"Globally in 2023, an average of 14.5% of life was spent in poor health, compared to 13.6% in 1990," the researchers at the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington reported.
JANE SEYMOUR, 75, SHARES HOW SHE APPROACHES AGING WITH VITALITY: 'BEST I CAN BE'
In the United States, the morbidity gap is about 14 years, or 17.8% of the expected lifespan.

"Between 1990 and 2023, global life expectancy at birth increased from 64.6 years to 73.8 years, while healthy life expectancy rose from 55.9 years to 63.1 years," the researchers reported in a news release.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
"Because gains in survival consistently outpaced gains in healthy years of life, people are spending more years living with chronic disease and disability."
A recent study found that the number of years people spend in poor health is widening, especially in America. (iStock)

The gap widened the most in the wealthiest countries where populations have access to life-extending resources, the researchers reported. Women are also living longer than men but are also spending more years in poor health, they found.

"To me, the most important message of this study is not that people are living longer. It is that we have become far better at delaying death than delaying functional decline," Dr. Antony Chu, clinical assistant professor at Brown University’s Warren Alpert School of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.

"Modern medicine has achieved remarkable success in reducing mortality from cardiovascular disease, cancer, trauma and infectious illness," he added. "Yet many of those additional years are now lived with chronic pain, disability, sensory loss, depression or reduced independence."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Researchers analyzed Global Burden of Disease data covering 204 countries and territories from 1990 through 2023. In their report, published by The Lancet Public Health, scientists observed that a small number of chronic, largely non-fatal causes were the primary contributors to the morbidity gap.

Musculoskeletal disorders, especially low back pain; mental disorders, such as depression and anxiety; hearing loss, falls and other non-communicable accounted for about 57% of all years lived in poor health worldwide. High fasting plasma glucose, obesity and aging populations were also important contributors.
The researchers noted that the study points to broad health trends but doesn’t prove exactly what's causing people to spend more years in poor health.
Researchers recently found people are spending more years living with chronic diseases and disabilities. (iStock)

"Our findings suggest that future gains in population health will come not only from helping people live longer, but from helping them live healthier," said Dr. Christopher Murray, director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington School of Medicine and senior author of the study.

"Progress in healthy aging should be measured not only by lifespan, but by healthspan [the number of years spent in good health], with greater investment in prevention, long-term disease management and chronic care to reduce years lived in poor health."

The goal should no longer be simply extending lifespan, but compressing morbidity and maximizing the number of years people remain physically, cognitively and socially well, Chu told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Ultimately, I believe the next frontier of medicine is not simply adding years to life, but adding life to years," he said. "First, we need to focus on preserving function rather than simply reacting to disease."

The approach involves routinely assessing mobility, muscle strength, balance, hearing, cognition and overall physical resilience. Chu said this may prove just as important as monitoring blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose.
"Functional decline often begins years before disability becomes obvious, providing an opportunity for earlier intervention," he said.
Many older Americans are socially isolated, though research shows relationships are important to longevity, an expert said. (iStock)
Musculoskeletal health also deserves much greater emphasis, Chu said.

"Progressive resistance training, fall prevention, maintenance of muscle mass and early treatment of chronic back pain should become core components of preventive medicine rather than afterthoughts," he said. "Preserving mobility may ultimately have as much impact on healthy aging as preventing heart disease."
Mental health and social connection are another vital component to healthspan, Chu said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Hearing loss, depression, anxiety and loneliness frequently reinforce one another, accelerating physical decline while diminishing quality of life," he said. "Addressing these conditions early may improve both longevity and independence."
Chu, who is the child of immigrants, said it’s his belief that Americans often overlook an important cultural dimension of healthy aging.

"In many societies outside the United States, older adults continue to play an active and respected role within multigenerational families," he said. "They remain mentors, caregivers, historians and sources of wisdom. This continued sense of purpose and belonging may provide meaningful protection against loneliness, depression and loss of identity.
A continued sense of purpose and belonging may lead people to live longer and healthier lives, according to an expert. (iStock)

"By contrast, many older Americans experience increasing social isolation precisely when maintaining meaningful relationships may be most important," Chu added. "Healthy aging is not determined solely by biology; it is also shaped by community, purpose and human connection."
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: 'Fit Mom' did 'everything right' — then a colon cancer diagnosis changed her life
summary: Maria Kang, the viral "No Excuses Mom" fitness influencer, reveals how Stage 4 colon cancer blindsided her despite years of healthy living.
story: Maria Kang told Fox News Digital she thought healthy eating and regular exercise would protect her until a Stage 4 colon cancer diagnosis revealed a different reality.

Maria Kang built her career around fitness, healthy eating and helping other moms prioritize wellness. Despite believing she had done "everything right," the California mother of three was blindsided by colon cancer.
Kang, now 46, said the diagnosis reshaped her understanding of what it means to be healthy.
She became an internet sensation in 2013 after a photo of her sculpted physique alongside her three young sons sparked a global conversation about fitness and motherhood.
LEADING ONCOLOGIST REVEALS 6 HABITS THAT COULD PROMOTE LONGEVITY AND REDUCE YOUR RISK OF CHRONIC ILLNESS
The viral image — captioned "What’s your excuse?" — led to her being dubbed the "No Excuse Mom" and inspired the launch of hundreds of wellness communities around the world.
More than a decade later, Kang’s world was turned upside down when she learned that she had Stage 4 colon cancer in November 2023.
Maria Kang built her career around fitness, healthy eating and helping other moms prioritize wellness but then was blindsided by colon cancer. (Beth Baugher, Maria Kang)

"It was definitely a complete shock because I was the healthiest person I knew," she shared with Fox News Digital. "I wanted to blame the food, but I didn't eat bad food. I filtered my water. There was no excuse why I had this cancer."
Looking back, Kang said she had experienced persistent digestive problems since adolescence, including chronic constipation and bloating that worsened with stress.
PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS
"It didn't matter how many fiber pills or laxatives, it just took a long time to go," she said. "So, that's been an ongoing journey throughout my life."
Over the years, Kang said, she convinced herself that her digestive problems were just something she had to live with.
Kang became an internet sensation in 2013 after a photo of her sculpted physique alongside her three young sons sparked a global conversation about fitness and motherhood. (Mike Byerly)

"One thing that I realized is that we normalize problems, and we think it's OK, but it’s not OK," she said. "Digestion should be like breathing. It should be like inhaling and exhaling. It should be simple. But it wasn't simple."

After a tumor was detected through a biopsy after a colonoscopy, Kang said she initially pursued holistic approaches for 12 weeks, but the tumor did not shrink and may have grown slightly. She then began FOLFOX, a combination of chemotherapy drugs used to treat some gastrointestinal cancers, in 2024.
MELINDA FRENCH GATES SAYS IT TOOK 3 DOCTORS TO DIAGNOSE THE CONDITION SHE WAS SUFFERING FROM

After one treatment, Kang went to the emergency room when her colostomy stoma retracted, and a scan reportedly showed that the tumor had shrunk substantially. She then asked to stop chemotherapy and proceed with surgery.

Kang later underwent extensive surgery to remove the tumor and about a foot of her colon, along with multiple reproductive organs and her appendix. She temporarily required a colostomy and later an ileostomy.
"It was definitely a complete shock because I was the healthiest person I knew."
Today, Kang says her MRIs have shown "no suspicious mass detected." She gets regular blood screenings and scans every six months.

"Much of what remains appears related to postoperative healing and inflammation," she shared. "Because of my history, my doctors continue surveillance, but I have not been formally declared NED (no evidence of disease)."
Alarming trends
An estimated 158,850 Americans will be diagnosed with colorectal cancer in 2026, and around 55,230 people will die from the disease this year, according to the American Cancer Society.

Although colorectal cancer incidence has declined overall — largely among older adults, a trend linked in part to increased screening and changes in certain risk factors — rates are rising in younger age groups.
Kang said her fitness and nutrition regimens also look drastically different from her pre-cancer routines. (Maria Kang)
Among adults younger than 50, colorectal cancer incidence increased by 2.9% per year from 2013 to 2022.

The American Cancer Society and U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommend that people at average risk begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45, although those with certain risk factors may need to start earlier.
Anyone experiencing persistent or concerning symptoms should consult a doctor, regardless of age.
‘I look healthy’
"It was a really big, humbling look in the mirror when you say to yourself, 'I look healthy, but I'm not healthy,’" Kang told Fox News Digital.
"When someone is at a normal range in their weight, they could have cancer. They could have autoimmune issues.
DOCTORS PUSH NEW BLOOD TESTS FOR COLON CANCER AS CASES SURGE IN YOUNGER ADULTS
"We don't know what's going on inside of a person. We always just want to look the part versus be the part."
Wellness redefined
Kang said her cancer journey has changed her perception of health and what’s important in life.

"Cancer makes everything extremely clear — what's important, what is not important, what you should eat, what you shouldn't eat," she said. "If you really listen to yourself, it becomes crystal clear when you have no energy."
Kang’s world was turned upside down when she learned that she had Stage 4 colon cancer in November 2023. (Maria Kang)
Kang said her fitness and nutrition regimens also look drastically different from her pre-cancer routines.

"I used to train five or six days a week, but now I only move when I want to," she said. "Walking is my best friend. I love to dance. I still love to strength-train because it's fun for me and it makes me strong."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Perhaps the biggest shift is that Kang no longer does anything that feels forced.
"If there's anything that I feel forced to do, I don't do it," she said. "If I feel awful, my body's going to express awful."
Her approach to food has also shifted, she shared.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"In the past, there were bad foods and good foods and cheat days … what I understand now is balance," Kang said.
While she does naturally veer toward fruits and vegetables — "things that have water and life and light in them" — Kang said she is still open to eating any other foods, including pizza.
Kang underwent extensive surgery to remove the tumor and about a foot of her colon, along with multiple reproductive organs and her appendix. (Maria Kang)
Overall, Kang wants people to know that maintaining healthy habits does not eliminate the possibility of developing cancer.
"It could happen to anybody. That was the most humbling realization," she said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"You may think you're young and healthy and this won't happen to you, but this world is so unpredictable right now. Anything can happen to anybody.
"Health is not what you think it is," she said. "It's not just how you look. It's how you feel."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The American Cancer Society recommends seeing a healthcare provider about persistent changes in bowel habits, blood in the stool, abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss or other concerning gastrointestinal symptoms.
While such symptoms can have many causes other than cancer, they should be evaluated regardless of a person’s age.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Measles surge hits new milestone as US cases surpass last year's total
summary: U.S. measles cases in 2026 have officially surpassed 2025 totals, with 93% of patients unvaccinated or unknown for MMR as outbreaks persist.
story: Dr. Nicole Saphier discusses the significant measles outbreak in Spartanburg County, South Carolina, with declining vaccination rates across the U.S.
Measles has reemerged as a persistent public health challenge in the U.S. over the past two years — and the spread isn't slowing down.
According to a Johns Hopkins University tracker that compiles local and state health data, there were 2,295 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. as of July 22.
This figure has officially surpassed the 2025 numbers, which totaled 2,286 measles cases nationwide.
MEASLES-INFECTED TRAVELER MAY HAVE EXPOSED PASSENGERS AT LAX AND NEARBY HOTEL, HEALTH OFFICIALS WARN
Cases have been reported across the country, but concentrated outbreaks have worsened in some areas of Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Florida, Virginia, Utah, Texas and Arizona.
In 2025, Texas had the largest outbreak — totaling 803 cases throughout the state.
Measles cases have officially surpassed 2025 numbers, which totaled 2,286 cases. The U.S. has reported 2,295 measles cases so far in 2026. (iStock)

In the latest CDC measles update on July 17, there were 34 new outbreaks reported in 2026, compared to 48 outbreaks in 2025. Most cases were associated with local outbreaks, while some were linked to international visitors.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Both this year and last year, 93% of all measles patients were either unvaccinated for measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), or had an unknown vaccination status, data shows.
Most cases have occurred in children and young adults between the ages of 5 and 19.
There have been no deaths reported in 2026, according to the CDC, but there were three deaths in 2025.

Most cases have occurred in children and young adults between the ages of 5 and 19. There have been no deaths reported in 2026, according to the CDC, but there were three deaths in 2025. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
The rise in cases comes more than two decades after health agencies reported that the disease was eliminated in 2000.

Measles can be spread through direct contact with infectious droplets, or can be airborne when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, according to health officials. The virus can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Symptoms usually appear within a week or two, and may include a high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes.
A few days later, flat, red spots appear on the face and then spread down the neck to the rest of the body. People are most contagious in the four days before and four days after the rash appears.
Community protection
Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, emphasized the highly contagious nature of measles.

"Measles is so contagious that up to 90% of susceptible people who are exposed to an infected person will become infected," he told Fox News Digital, noting the importance of community protection. "We need a 95% vaccine coverage rate to ensure herd immunity," he said.
A paramedic administers a dose of the measles vaccine at a health center in Lubbock, Texas, on Feb. 27, 2025. (RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP via Getty Images)
The herd immunity threshold is a mathematical estimate based on how contagious a disease is and how effectively immunity from vaccination or prior infection prevents its spread, according to Siegel.

"In this case, two-dose vaccination is almost 100% effective, and natural immunity after a measles infection is generally lifelong," the doctor said. "This isn’t about personal choice, it’s about community protection. We need to protect those who can’t have a live virus vaccine because they are immunocompromised or pregnant."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The doctor also cautioned that the U.S. could be at risk of losing its measles elimination status, as the number and duration of outbreaks suggest sustained local transmission within the U.S., rather than isolated cases linked only to international travel.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The CDC recommends that everyone receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, calling vaccination the best protection against measles.
Anyone who is showing measles symptoms or thinks they’ve been exposed should self-isolate and contact their doctor before showing up to a medical center and infecting others.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Sharon Stone's terrifying weed withdrawal sparks warning about today's potent marijuana
summary: Sharon Stone's marijuana withdrawal symptoms were so severe that she saw a neurologist, highlighting the dangers of quitting high-potency THC without a plan.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses new research that casts doubt on cannabis benefits and highlights increased mental health risks, especially for teenagers. Modern marijuana, with 70-90% THC potency, is linked to higher rates of PTSD, anxiety, depression, ADHD, and bipolar disorder. Usage among Americans aged 12 and older has skyrocketed by 180% since the early 2000s, leading to concerns about addiction and health issues.
Hollywood icon Sharon Stone recently opened up about a health scare after quitting marijuana, revealing her symptoms were so intense that she turned to a neurologist.
During an interview with Variety, the actress said her decision to quit was driven by a desire for a drug-free life.
"And because I think they put so much stuff in it now — they really do — when I stopped smoking pot, I also got sick," she said.
CANNABIS COMPOUNDS COULD REVERSE DISEASE AFFECTING ONE-THIRD OF ADULTS
"I got pretty sick for a month. I went to my neurologist, and he said, ‘Sharon, I’ve had people dying in the emergency room from marijuana.'"
Stone attributed her ordeal to the potency of modern weed, saying, "It’s not like you’re pulling it out of the ground anymore ... It’s not like when we were kids."
American actress Sharon Stone quit "smoking pot" and got so sick that she consulted a neurologist, she revealed in a recent interview. (Getty Images, iStock)

Experts note that cannabis withdrawal itself is generally not considered life-threatening, although severe symptoms, underlying medical conditions or interactions with other substances can complicate recovery.
FLYING WITH CANNABIS? TSA'S NEW GUIDANCE COMES WITH A MAJOR HEALTH WARNING
Dr. Chris Tuell, clinical director of addiction services at the Lindner Center in Cincinnati, confirmed that today's cannabis products are vastly different from the strains of decades past.
THC levels in marijuana have surged from about 3% to 5% in the 1980s to as high as 30% in today's cannabis products, while concentrates can exceed 90% THC, he told Fox News Digital.
"I do believe cannabis is addicting, especially with the high levels of THC."

Higher THC concentrations have been linked to greater risks of dependence, cannabis use disorder (CUD), psychosis in some users and more severe withdrawal symptoms, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse.

As today's cannabis products become increasingly potent, experts say there are several risks and warning signs that daily users should know before deciding whether to continue — or quit — using marijuana.
No. 1: High-potency THC changes the brain's reward system
According to Cleveland Clinic, CUD occurs when marijuana takes over the brain's reward pathways, amplifying compulsive behavior.
"I do believe cannabis is addicting, especially with the high levels of THC," Tuell told Fox News Digital.
No. 2: Addiction isn't always obvious

The American Psychiatric Association’s DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition) outlines the following diagnostic criteria signaling that casual use may have crossed into dependency.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Taking larger amounts over longer periods than intendedExperiencing unsuccessful attempts to cut down or control usageFailing to fulfill work, school or home responsibilitiesContinuing use despite clear relationship problems
Taking larger amounts over longer periods than intended
Experiencing unsuccessful attempts to cut down or control usage
Failing to fulfill work, school or home responsibilities
Continuing use despite clear relationship problems
Today’s cannabis flower and concentrates contain up to 90% THC, making modern products exponentially stronger than those from decades past, experts say. (iStock)
No. 3: Withdrawal can be intense
Quitting heavy, long-term cannabis use can trigger withdrawal symptoms within 24 to 48 hours, Cleveland Clinic notes.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Users frequently experience severe insomnia, intense irritability, anxiety, appetite loss, sweating, headaches and stomach upset. While acute physical symptoms typically resolve within a month, mood swings and sleep issues can linger much longer, according to Tuell.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
4. Medical guidance may be needed

While cannabis withdrawal alone rarely requires hospitalization, Cleveland Clinic notes that people with significant medical or mental health conditions — or those stopping cannabis while also withdrawing from alcohol, opioids or certain other medications — may benefit from medical supervision.
Addiction experts strongly advise stepping down THC intake slowly to cushion the impact on the nervous system and avoid severe rebound symptoms. (iStock)
No. 5: Underlying issues may fuel dependence

Mental health conditions often occur alongside cannabis use disorder, and treating those underlying issues may help reduce problematic marijuana use, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Cleveland Clinic.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"I strongly believe that CUD and mental health issues co-exist, and that mental health counseling can address the issues driving the addictive behaviors," Tuell said.
Fox News Digital reached out to Stone's representatives requesting comment.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Clinton, Obama-era Democratic heavyweights Penn and Emanuel rip NYC's Mamdani over taxes, Israel, blast DSA
summary: Democratic power players Mark Penn and Rahm Emanuel publicly criticize NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his property tax plan and Israel positions.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces backlash after rolling out a new ‘Pied-à-Terre’ tax and publishing a searchable database of property owners, raising concerns over privacy, economic impacts and the treatment of homeowners and investors.

Two prominent Democratic figures with deep ties to the Clinton and Obama administrations publicly criticized New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani this week, with former Clinton adviser Mark Penn attacking the mayor's proposed property tax plan while former Obama White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel recounted what he described as a private conversation in which he challenged Mamdani's rhetoric on Israel.

The criticism is notable because it comes from longtime Democrat insiders rather than Republican opponents and focuses on two of the issues that have defined Mamdani's rise political rise: his far-left economic agenda and his positions on Israel.
Fox News Digital reached out to Penn, Emanuel and Mamdani's office for comment.
NYC MAYOR MAMDANI CALLS THREAT OF RICH PEOPLE LEAVING NYC OVER TAXES 'IMAGINED'
Mark Penn participates in a panel discussion during the annual Milken Institute Global Conference at The Beverly Hilton Hotel on April 29, 2019, in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Getty Images)

Penn, a longtime Democrat strategist and former pollster and adviser to President Bill Clinton, accused Mamdani of dramatically understating the scope of his proposed pied-à-terre tax after the mayor released a public database identifying property owners who could be subject to it.

In a lengthy post on X, Penn argued the city's valuation system had swept in nearly one million property owners rather than the roughly 30,000 luxury homeowners Penn said had previously been described as the intended targets.
"The $5 million figure was a fake," Penn wrote, arguing the city's valuation system had improperly classified properties and would force homeowners to prove they should not be taxed.
RAHM EMANUEL WARNS NEW GENERATION OF DEM SOCIALISTS DON'T LIKE AMERICA

Former Mayor of Chicago and White House Chief of Staff Rahm Emanuel speaks during the 29th annual Milken Institute Global Conference at the Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills, California on May 5, 2026. ((Photo by Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images))
Penn also argued the proposal could depress property values, discourage investment in New York City and potentially raise constitutional questions.

Meanwhile, Emanuel said during an appearance on the Unholy Podcast that he met privately with Mamdani for roughly 90 minutes and challenged the self-described democratic socialist mayor over his views on Israel.
Emanuel said he praised portions of Mamdani's domestic agenda, including childcare, but criticized Mamdani's past use of the phrase "from the river to the sea."
MAMDANI DODGES ON ‘POLITICAL THEATER’ OF EMPTY NETANYAHU ARREST THREAT, CALLS FOR US ACTION AND NYC PROTESTS

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's video admitting that he lacks the legal authority to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did little to ease Jewish leaders' concerns. (NYC Mayor's Office via YouTube/Handout via Reuters)
"I know where there's a line. You don't," Emanuel recalled telling Mamdani.
Emanuel said both calls for a "Greater Israel" and the slogan "from the river to the sea" would lead to "perpetual conflict."
After clips of Emanuel's remarks circulated online, Mamdani communications director Anna Bahr publicly disputed the account.
"can confirm this .... did not happen," Bahr wrote on X in response to a post summarizing Emanuel's remarks.
It was not immediately clear from Bahr's post whether she was disputing that the meeting occurred or Emanuel's characterization of the conversation.

Emanuel has also recently criticized the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) more broadly. In a post on X this week, he argued Democrats should focus on winning competitive elections rather than what he characterized as ideological distractions.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"You can be focused on winning tough races, flipping red seats blue. Or you can be focused on abolishing prisons and... the Senate and Supreme Court? You can't do both," Emanuel wrote. "I'm for winning this November and ending Trump's corruption — and I'm also for putting an end to all the distractions from the DSA."
Penn, Emanuel and Mamdani's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for additional comment before publication.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Trump AG pick Blanche stalled as key Republicans refuse to budge
summary: Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis demanded written proposals to modify the Trump IRS settlement, derailing Todd Blanche's confirmation vote.
story: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche faces renewed scrutiny during his Senate confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill.
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s chances of confirmation were derailed Wednesday, less than 24 hours before a pivotal vote in the Senate.

It’s another chapter in the troubled saga that has followed Blanche since he was tapped to replace former Attorney General Pam Bondi and one that boils down to issues among Blanche, the Department of Justice (DOJ) and two key Republicans who control his fate in the Senate Judiciary Committee.

Senators John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., are demanding that the DOJ provide explicit, written proposals to modify the settlement deal reached between the IRS and President Donald Trump and his family earlier this year.
TRUMP AG PICK TODD BLANCHE FACES SENATE TEST IN FIRST MAJOR CONFIRMATION FIGHT SINCE GRAHAM’S DEATH
Todd Blanche, nominee for U.S. deputy attorney general, testifies before the Senate Judiciary Committee in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 12, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., had hoped a deal could be struck and allow for the confirmation to move forward, eying next week as the major floor vote to formally confirm Blanche as Bondi's replacement.

"I think that that's an issue between, right now, the White House and Senators Cornyn and Tillis," Thune said. "But, yeah, I would encourage them to sit down, which I think they are, and try to come to a resolution there so that the markup can continue tomorrow, and we can get Todd Blanche ready for the floor."
The DOJ had until 4 p.m. Wednesday to get the lawmakers what they wanted, but the agency fell short, and Blanche’s bumpy carriage ride to confirmation turned into a pumpkin.
Without a guarantee that Cornyn or Tillis would vote to confirm Blanche, Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, opted to postpone the hearing until a later date.

Their targets are the now-defunct, nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund and the president’s audit immunity. Republicans and Democrats alike railed against the fund, particularly over concerns that the funding would go to people involved in the Jan. 6, 2021, riots on Capitol Hill.

Trump's audit immunity has similarly ruffled feathers. Blanche, in his announcement of the settlement deal earlier this year, outlined that, as part of the agreement, the IRS would not be allowed to audit Trump, his family or affiliated companies.
DEMS REJECT TRUMP’S TOP SPY PICK AFTER DEMANDING REPLACEMENT, LEAVING COUNTER-TERROR TOOL IN AIR
Cornyn has proven the most resistant until his demands are met. He's used his newfound freedom to extract concessions from the Trump administration in recent weeks.

His push for an explicit end to the audit language in the settlement agreement is another such example. The longtime lawmaker, who will exit the Senate at the end of this year after being ousted by the Trump-backed Ken Paxton, was set to meet Blanche Wednesday morning.

But the confab was called off, and Blanche continued making the rounds in the Senate throughout the day, capping off his visit to the Capitol with Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo. He declined to comment to reporters on his way out.
Cornyn said it was "made clear from the outset that we expected some written proposals to modify the release that was signed in the tax dispute with President Trump and his organization."

"We need to conform the actual document to what Todd Blanche testified under oath as the president's acting attorney general," Cornyn said. "We've had two meetings scheduled that have now been canceled because they have not been responsive in providing those written documents."
TRUMP AG PICK HANGS BY A THREAD AS KEY GOP SENATORS REFUSE TO COMMIT
Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, departs a meeting with Senate Republicans at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., June 4, 2026. (Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump, when asked about the holdup in the Senate for Blanche, portrayed himself as a president at an arm's length from the situation and said he heard his attorney general pick was "going through quite nicely."

"Well, all I can say is Todd Blanche is outstanding. And I thought he's — I thought it was pretty routine because he's so good," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "You just wouldn't find a better person. So, I don't know, maybe John Cornyn is upset with me because I didn't endorse him. I don't know what it is, but I haven't heard that there's a problem."
Tillis made clear he doesn't "have a beef with DOJ or with Blanche."
"They're trying to get it done, but still gotta get it done," Tillis said.

He also noted that the number of hurdles that getting those kinds of written proposals through was more extensive than meets the eye. For example, Tillis said the actual settlement likely was signed by the president's lawyer and not Trump himself.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"So there's, you know, there's a circle of people that have to go through the loop," he said. "And I get that, but, you know, if we can get it done or possibly get him reported out on Tuesday, if they schedule a markup, I would support that if we get the language."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Ted Cruz demands Fauci face jail time, labels him America's 'most damaging bureaucrat'
summary: Ted Cruz says Anthony Fauci should face contempt charges, perjury prosecution and jail after pleading the Fifth over 100 times at a Senate hearing.
story: Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, blasts former COVID-19 advisor Anthony Fauci, backing efforts to hold him in contempt and arguing he should face jail time for misleading the American people about the virus. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, is calling for Anthony Fauci to be held in contempt, prosecuted for perjury and sent to jail after the former White House COVID-19 advisor pleaded his Fifth Amendment right more than 100 times during a Senate hearing Wednesday.
"Years from now, they'll look back and say, ‘What collective madness overtook this country?’" Cruz told Fox News Digital.

"I think Anthony Fauci has had contempt for Congress and contempt for the American people for decades," he said. "His diary shows that he deliberately lied to the American people over and over and over again."
FAUCI PLEADS FIFTH WITH 'ZERO LEGAL JUSTIFICATION' AS CRITICS ERUPT AND DEMAND CONTEMPT CHARGES

Anthony Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and medical advisor to several U.S. presidents, testifies under subpoena about his role in the national response to the COVID-19 pandemic at a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., July 29, 2026. (Reuters/Nathan Howard)

Cruz made the comments after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul announced he will seek contempt charges against Fauci after Fauci dodged self-incrimination by refusing to answer any questions throughout the entirety of the hearing.
"Dr. Fauci ought to think about what it says about the end of his career, that what he will be remembered for the most is pleading the Fifth more than 100 times," Cruz said.
"He's been the most damaging bureaucrat in the history of America."
RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas., is calling for Anthony Fauci to be held in contempt and sent to jail after his Senate hearing on Wednesday for his alleged dishonesty about COVID-19 to both Congress and the American people. (Nicholas Ballasy/Fox News Digital)

Cruz and Fauci have had a longstanding feud, similar to his relationships with other GOP senators like Paul, over Fauci’s handling of the outbreak and claims he was dishonest about the origins of COVID-19 to both Congress and the American people.

"In his diary, he wrote early on that it was clear that the COVID virus did not come from the wet market in Wuhan, and then he turned around and said exactly the opposite thing on national television," Cruz said.

The released private diaries expose that Fauci considered possibilities about how the virus originated that he later downplayed to the public. He wrote that scientists considered the possibility of a deliberately inserted laboratory origin worthy of further expert review, while his later statements suggested the opposite to the public.
LEGACY MEDIA IGNORES MASSIVE ANTHONY FAUCI DOCUMENT RELEASE ALLEGING HE MISLED CONGRESS ON COVID ORIGINS

The Texas senator also accused Fauci of pushing for the lockdown of schools. Fauci wrote in his diary that he convinced both New York and California government officials to lock down their state’s school systems. This was, again, contradictory to what he said publicly, when he claimed multiple times in interviews and testified to the House Oversight Committee that he "did not close the schools."
"In his diary, he brags about convincing Democrats in New York and California to shut schools down, and yet he goes on TV and says, ‘Oh, I wasn't for shutdowns,’" Cruz said.

"The school shutdowns, which Fauci bragged that he was responsible for, may well be the single most destructive public policy step we've seen in decades. That learning loss will stick with those kids the rest of their lives when they're 90 years old.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"They will still be suffering the consequences of Anthony Fauci's corrupt and dishonest shutdowns.
"The fact that he knew he was lying to the American people — he should be held in contempt, he should be prosecuted for perjury, and he should go to jail."
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: El-Sayed in the hot seat for another foreign rental property, nearly $300K in additional income
summary: Abdul El-Sayed released tax disclosures just hours before a debate, revealing a Dubai rental property and total assets worth up to $2.1 million.
story: Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., accused Democratic Senate rival Abdul El-Sayed of withholding his full tax returns while earning $300,000 in outside income and promoting what she called ‘junk health care cures’ through his podcast. (Credit: WJBK)

Moments ahead of a primary debate Monday night, Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed released a new financial disclosure, revealing new details about he and his wife’s assets worth up to $2.1 million.

The disclosures, which come a week ahead of a heated primary election between El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., shed new light on El-Sayed’s finances, but questions still remain about the specifics of his wealth.
While, broadly, much of the information was already known through reporting he did last year, the 2026 filing adds three key additions.
El Sayed and his wife listed a rental property in Dubai worth up to $250,000, a liability to a company in Dubai worth up to $100,000 and a tweak to El-Sayed’s employment status in Michigan.
SOCIALIST-BACKED DEM WHO RIPPED THE WEALTHY CRACKS STATE’S TOP 1%, TAX RETURNS SHOW
Abdul El-Sayed, candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks before U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., takes the stage at Mumford High School May 3, 2026, in Detroit. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)
Past reporting had already shown that El-Sayed’s wife owned a rental property in Ann Harbor, Michigan, and another in Bangalore, India.

The Dubai property is a third real estate holding. The debt, worth between $50,000 and $100,000, is a liability owed to Majid Al Futtaim Tilal, a real estate development company that specializes in luxury residential projects.

And, finally, the filing adds that El-Sayed worked as a consultant for Wayne County, Michigan, with an income of $72,000. At the same time, the filing lists a salary of $82,750, also for Wayne County. The consulting is a change from a salaried position listed at $278,900 the year before.
"Know many people who own rental properties in three countries?" prominent gun-control activist Shannon Watts posted on X.
"Why are all the socialists rich????" Democratic analyst Rachel Bitecofer posted on X.
The 2025 and 2026 filings put El-Sayed’s net worth between $870,000 and $2.1 million.

The Michigan race has drawn national attention as Stevens, a more establishment candidate with the backing of Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., squares off against El-Sayed’s progressive promises to challenge the U.S.-Israel relationship, abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and provide universal healthcare. His platform has drawn support from fellow progressives such as Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.
WATCH: SURFACED VIDEOS OF DEM SENATE CANDIDATE BACKING 'DEFUND THE POLICE' CONTRADICT RECENT DENIALS
Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., a Michigan U.S. Senate candidate, speaks with the media after a debate at WoodTV studios July 7, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Kristen Norman)

With a groundswell of support among progressives, Stevens has sought to paint El-Sayed as a far cry from the middle-class working-family base he claims to champion, needling El-Sayed over his net worth in a debate last month.
"Look, I am the only one running for United States Senate in Michigan who is not a millionaire," Stevens said at the time.
At the debate Monday, Stevens mentioned the filings and what she characterized as a lack of transparency.

"You have not released your tax returns," Stevens reminded him. "You talk about getting money out of politics and putting money in people’s pockets, but still no one knows who’s putting the money in your pocket."
El-Sayed, who filed the Senate report right before the debate, said he had made the necessary disclosures, sidestepping the comment about his tax returns.
DEM PRIMARY ERUPTS AS ESTABLISHMENT FAVORITE DISMISSES RIVAL AS ‘CELEBRITY CANDIDATE’
Abdul El-Sayed, a candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks before U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., takes the stage at Mumford High School May 3, 2026, in Detroit. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"This is a distraction from the issues in your life," he said at Monday’s debate.

El-Sayed’s most recent disclosures follow an application for an extension that allowed him an extra 90 days to finalize his 2026 paperwork. That extension would have allowed him to submit his disclosures on Aug. 13, a week after the primary. When confronted about the timeline, El-Sayed pledged on a podcast earlier this month to submit his disclosures before the election.
El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the disclosures or the timing of its submission.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Trump taps veterans to fix illegal alien trucking problem plaguing US roadways
summary: Trump's Freedom Haulers initiative expands CDL eligibility for military veterans while removing over 24,000 improperly licensed commercial drivers.
story: Fox News' Kevin Corke reports on a joint investigation by the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Transportation targeting truck driver schools. The probe addresses improper certifications and falsified records, especially concerning the issuance of commercial driver's licenses to non-citizens/

FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump will launch the White House's new Freedom Haulers initiative Thursday, Fox News Digital has exclusively learned, opening new pathways for military veterans to become commercial truck drivers while intensifying the administration's crackdown on illegal immigrant and non-English-speaking truckers.

"President Trump’s administration has made our roads safer by taking illegal alien, non-English-speaking truck drivers off America’s highways. Now, through the Freedom Haulers initiative, the president is expanding opportunities for our veterans by making it easier to obtain commercial driver’s licenses once they conclude their service," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Fox News Digital.
The Trump administration is pairing its crackdown on illegal immigrants and non-English-speaking commercial drivers with a new effort to recruit military veterans into the trucking industry.

Trump, along with Department of Transportation (DOT) Secretary Sean Duffy, Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins and acting Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, will welcome a truck on West Executive Avenue to announce the initiative.
JOE BIDEN MANDATED ALL NEW VEHICLES COME INSTALLED WITH A 'KILL SWITCH.' THIS REPUBLICAN WANTS TO REPEAL IT

Former President Donald Trump, the Republican presidential nominee, holds a news conference from inside trash hauler at Green Bay Austin Straubel International Airport Oct. 30, 2024. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"By leading a multi-agency process spanning the departments of Transportation, Labor, Veterans Affairs and War, President Trump is bolstering America’s trucking industry, which is crucial to strong supply chains, while helping our nation’s heroes transition to civilian life with quality, good-paying jobs," Kelly added.

The Department of Transportation will expand eligibility for veterans to receive expedited commercial driver's licenses (CDLs), extending the waiver period from 12 months to 24 months after active-duty service.
For veterans who have never driven a heavy commercial vehicle during their military service, CDL training will be offered.
ILLEGAL TRUCKER CASES FUEL GOP PUSH TO CRACK DOWN ON CDL MILLS AS DEMS LARGELY SILENT

Former President Donald Trump, the Republican presidential nominee, holds a news conference from inside a trash hauler at Green Bay Austin Straubel International Airport Oct. 30, 2024. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Indiana and Wyoming will also join the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration's Even Exchange program, allowing military truck drivers to more easily transition into civilian CDLs.
Werner Enterprises, an Omaha, Nebraska-based trucking company attending Thursday's event, will announce plans to hire 1,400 new veteran drivers.
The administration is also highlighting its ongoing crackdown on commercial drivers who fail to meet English-language proficiency requirements or are improperly licensed.
VIRGINIA BUS CRASH THAT KILLED FIVE INVOLVED DRIVER WHO DOESN'T SPEAK ENGLISH, SEAN DUFFY SAYS
Trucks travel on Interstate 80 Nov. 14, 2025, in Albany, Calif. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
The Department of Transportation says it has removed more than 24,000 commercial driver's licenses from the nation's highways under stricter English-language proficiency enforcement.
More than 28,000 CDLs were also canceled after officials determined they had been improperly issued to noncitizen truck drivers.
The White House says the initiative is aimed at improving highway safety while strengthening the nation's trucking workforce.
The announcement comes after a series of fatal crashes involving illegal immigrant truck drivers in states including Florida, California, Indiana and Pennsylvania.

Earlier this month, a Pennsylvania State Police trooper was killed during a roadside inspection when a semitruck driven by a Haitian national struck him. Authorities say the driver had obtained a non-domiciled CDL before the administration's rule changes.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Truck drivers have seen a 7.42% increase in real wages during the Trump administration, compared to a 3% decline in real wages under President Biden, according to DOT.

DOT also says veteran truck drivers experience 42% fewer accidents and cover 98% more miles than non-veteran drivers, arguing the initiative will both improve highway safety and help strengthen America's supply chains.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump family profits from blockbuster deal in Central Asia despite backlash due to 'proof problem': expert
summary: A securities attorney says the Trump brothers' investment in a company tied to a $1.6 billion Kazakhstan tungsten deal raises suspicions but lacks proof.
story: Securities and investment fraud attorney Andrew Stoltmann says an investment by the Trump brothers raises eyebrows.

The Trump Organization, led by President Donald Trump's sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, made a controversial investment in a construction company that now stands to profit from a rare earth minerals deal funded by the U.S. government.
While the deal raises suspicions, one securities attorney says evidence of wrongdoing is likely impossible to find and acknowledged that critics have a "proof problem."

"Well, the question is whether President Trump would have known about his sons’ investments in this company, and I think the answer would be ‘no’ unless the sons told them," Andrew Stoltmann, a Chicago-based securities and investment fraud attorney, told Fox News Digital.

"Look, they are private investors," he continued. "They are not government employees. So, to the extent they make a passive investment in a company or an entity, there are no real duties to disclose this information."

Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump look on as President Donald Trump and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen announce a U.S.-EU trade deal after a meeting at Trump Turnberry golf club July 27, 2025, in Turnberry, Scotland. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
RESOURCE-RICH NATION PRAISES US TIES AMID WASHINGTON-BEIJING CRITICAL MINERALS RACE

The controversy stems from a tungsten mining deal in Kazakhstan, which primarily involves U.S.-based investment company Cove Capital and the company's mining affiliate, Cove Kaz Capital Group. Between 2023 and 2024, Cove Capital negotiated with the Kazakh government to take a 70% share in the country's state-owned tungsten mining deposits.

Tungsten is a rare earth mineral that is critical to building military equipment, including missiles and fighter jets. The lion's share of the earth's supply of the mineral is owned by China and Russia. Trump, since returning to office, has made it a strategic national security priority to secure a long-term supply of the resource.

In August 2025, through an investment vehicle created by Dominari Securities, which is housed in Trump Tower in New York, the Trump brothers purchased a minority interest in a construction company, Skyline Builders, which at the time was publicly traded on the NASDAQ under the ticker SKBL.
U.S. President Donald Trump motions to reporters after getting off Air Force One on July 22, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Md. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
HOWARD LUTNICK SHUTS DOWN DEM QUESTIONS OVER JEFFREY EPSTEIN AT BUDGET HEARING

In June of that year, Cantor Fitzgerald, founded by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, underwrote a $46.8 million loan to a company called ASP Isotopes. ASP Isotopes is owned by businessman Paul Mann. Lutnick's company is now controlled by his sons, Brandon and Kyle Lutnick, who took over when their father became a government official.
At about the time of underwriting, the Trump brothers were investing in Skyline Builders, a wholly-owned ASP Isotopes subsidiary that acquired voting control of Skyline Builders.

On Nov. 6, 2025, Kazakhstan President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, met with Trump and announced that the Central Asian country had awarded a tungsten mining contract to the United States. The Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), which provide government financing for international projects, penned letters of interest totaling up to $1.6 billion in financing for the deal. Cove Kaz Capital was selected as the firm to do the majority of the mining.
The deal has not officially been inked and is under a standard review process by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
The wilderness and steppe landscape in Issyk-Kul lake region, a Jeti-Oguz and Tong district, Kyrgyzstan in Central Asia, with far view of town. (Getty Images)

Earlier this spring, Skyline Builders completed a reverse merger with Cove Kaz Capital, creating a company called Kaz Resources, which is now listed on the NASDAQ as KAZR. Skyline Builders owns 20% of Kaz Resources after a $20 million investment.
ERIC TRUMP PLANS TO SUE JEN PSAKI, MS NOW FOR ALLEGED 'BLATANT LIES' ABOUT HIM JOINING FATHER'S CHINA TRIP

Critics have suggested — albeit without evidence — that the Trump brothers schemed to invest in Skyline Builders with advance knowledge that Kazakhstan would opt to award the billion-and-a-half-dollar tungsten deal to the United States instead of other countries, and, in turn, Kaz Resources would secure the contract.

The Trump organization vehemently denies that characterization and says the investment made by the brothers through Dominari Securities in Skyline Builders was passive, made before the tungsten deal was done and made without the knowledge that Kazakhstan would award the mining contract to the United States in the first place.
Even without wrongdoing, Stoltmann said the appearance of impropriety could cause headaches.

"The $64,000 question is pretty much what Trump knew and when he knew it — and, look, the optics are bad," he said. "You have the president's sons investing in a company that is eventually awarded a very large contract, and so it certainly raises eyebrows, it raises suspicions.
"And it's certainly clear why this has caused an uproar. But a lot of times, this is more thunder, this is more noise — a tempest in a teapot, as I like to say."
An aerial drone photo shows grassland in the Akmola region in northern Kazakhstan Aug. 17, 2024. (Xinhua News Agency via Getty Images)

In discussing potential ramifications, Stoltmann said members of the political left who are frenzied over the deal will have trouble finding proof of wrongdoing, as Trump would have no way of knowing about his sons' investment unless they told him about it.
"But this is where the proof problem comes in," said Stoltmann.

"It's fun to have conjecture. It's fun to theorize, and it's fun to discuss this, but I don't think there's any duty of disclosure when you are a passive investor in a company, and that's where President Trump would most certainly say, 'I don't know all the things my sons do.'"

As for the Lutnick brothers, Stoltmann noted that Cantor Fitzgerald stood to financially benefit from underwriting and advisory fees when it helped finance the loan for Mann, whose company now owns a majority voting stake in Kaz Resources.

"You most certainly need a Wall Street brokerage firm or bank to help finance some of this, but, more importantly, to do the underwriting," Stoltmann said. "We have reverse mergers, we have mergers and we have multiple shell companies coming into the equation. When you do that, you need a bank, you need a brokerage firm. And that's where Cantor Fitzgerald comes in."
Howard Lutnick joined the Trump administration as Commerce Secretary in 2025 after co-chairing Trump’s transition team. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

In the way of political ramifications, Stoltmann warned that if Democrats regain control of the House and Senate in November, the Trump brothers will likely face heat from the president's political opponents for any business deals that they think can come under scrutiny.

"You're going see a tsunami of subpoenas trying to get the phone records, the communication records, the emails of the Trump boys and President Trump and everybody associated with this deal," he predicted. "So, look, is there potential legal liability this situation? Yes, there is. I don't think there is for President Trump, though.

"You know, clearly, at least by all appearances, it seems like his sons were passive investors, and the sons would say, ‘Look, we're worth a couple hundred million dollars. We have passive investments in dozens and dozens, if not hundreds of different companies. This is all pure than Caesar's wife,’ but it certainly raises some suspicions."
The White House reiterated that the president does not directly manage his investment holdings and that they are instead managed by independent third-party financial institutions.
The $16.5 billion nuclear plant project was signed during high-level talks in Astana between Putin and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. (Getty)

"This is the same, tired narrative that Democrats have pushed against President Trump, his family and his administration for a decade," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said. "President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public, which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses from the fake news media. There are no conflicts of interest."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Cantor Fitzgerald emphasized that it had no interaction at all with Kaz Resources or Skyline Builders.

"Cantor is a natural partner for companies raising capital to meet growing demand for critical minerals," a spokesperson said. "Cantor’s involvement is limited to supporting capital raises in the public markets and does not include participation in negotiations with the current or any prior administration."
The Trump Organization and Commerce Department did not return Fox News Digital's requests for comment.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Graham's final mission advances as Senate moves to crush Putin's war machine with Russia, Iran sanctions
summary: The sanctions package allows up to 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% tariffs on countries buying Russian energy, like China and India.
story: Shannon Bream discusses with senators Jeanne Shaheen and Katie Britt their bipartisan bill aimed at sanctioning Russia.
The Senate took another small step toward levying sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, the Kremlin and Iran in another massive, bipartisan vote.
Though not the final vote to pass the long-stalled effort, the latest successful bid to move a bone-crushing sanctions package once championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham is no less significant.

The upper chamber hopes to complete work on the package, renamed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, by next week. If successful, the long-awaited legislation will again be put on the shelf, albeit temporarily, until the House returns from its August recess.
'A BIG EFFING DEAL': GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION MOVES FORWARD AFTER HIS DEATH

Sen. Lindsey Graham mills about before President Donald Trump delivers the State of the Union address during a joint session of Congress at the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 24, 2026. (Kenny Holston/Pool/Getty Images)

Still, lawmakers are confident they can get the bill through the next few hurdles and believe that it’s the best way to honor Graham, who made his final trip home to South Carolina on Wednesday for his funeral.
"This may turn out to be Lindsey Graham's greatest legislative achievement in a stellar 32-year career," Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., said.

The bill, which has gone through several iterations, still focuses on kneecapping Putin’s war machine in its ongoing fight with Ukraine. However, it reinserts sanctions targeting Iran’s weapons and energy sectors in the hopes of incentivizing a lasting peace deal as the war in the Middle East marches on.
PUTIN, RUSSIA PUT ON NOTICE AS SENATE TAKES CRUCIAL STEP TO GRIND DOWN THE KREMLIN’S WAR MACHINE

Key components of the legislation allow for up to 500% tariffs on Russian imports; tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian energy, like China and India; and provides President Donald Trump flexibility for when to turn off some aspects of the sanctions.
Some Democrats have acknowledged that giving Trump tariff authority could give their colleagues heartburn, particularly after raging against his usage of duties during his second term.

Proponents of the bill brought in heavy artillery to convince Democratic skeptics in the form of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a close ally of Graham’s, to win some key votes for the package.
LINDSEY GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION NEARS FINISH LINE AS WORLD LEADERS GATHER TO HONOR HIM
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday said he thinks the war with Ukraine could end soon. (Alexander Nemenov/AFP)
Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., said on the Senate floor that she was aware that some had raised concerns about the tariff authorities.
"They say that President Trump has used tariffs indiscriminately to target our closest allies. Well, I agree," Shaheen said.

"But, in the case of this bill, Congress is explicitly directing these tariffs for one unambiguous purpose: to increase the pressure on Vladimir Putin and end his unprovoked war against Ukraine," she continued. "That’s why this bill is narrowly targeted at the worst actors supporting Russia."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
And at its core, the legislation is still meant to send Putin and the Kremlin a strong message as the war in Ukraine rages on.

"This bill says to Vladimir Putin, ‘Your days of war are numbered. You are on the losing side. Better to come to the table now than sacrifice more lives, waste more money, crater your economy, destroy your standing in the world,’" Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Fox News Poll: Democratic enthusiasm shapes North Carolina Senate race
summary: Roy Cooper leads Michael Whatley by 9 points in North Carolina's Senate race, but an enthusiasm gap and Trump's favorability could reshape the contest.
story: Fox News' power rankings reveal tight races in both the Senate and House, with 100 days remaining until the midterm elections. Four Senate seats and 16 House seats are toss-ups, indicating a highly competitive midterm election landscape.

In North Carolina, more Democrats than Republicans say they are extremely interested in the midterm elections (51% vs. 42%), and more Democrats also say they are extremely motivated to vote (58% vs. 50%). This enthusiasm advantage creates an edge in the Senate matchup.
Democrat Roy Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley by 53% to 44% in the race to fill the state’s open Senate seat, according to a Fox News poll of North Carolina voters.

Cooper’s gap widens to 15 points among those saying they’re extremely interested in the election (57% vs. 42%) and 13 points among those extremely motivated to vote (55% vs. 42%). The race is unchanged among those saying they’re "certain" to vote (53% to 44%).
FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS

Whatley is the former chair of the Republican National Committee, while Cooper served as North Carolina’s governor from 2017-2025. The candidates are vying to fill the seat held by retiring Republican Senator Thom Tillis.

Cooper receives high support from moderates, voters under age 30, independents, voters with a college degree, and women. He also captures support from about one in five non-MAGA Republicans and conservatives.
Whatley performs best among very conservative voters, White evangelical Christians, White voters without a college degree, and rural voters.

There’s also an enthusiasm gap when voters are asked why they back their candidate. Some 52% of Whatley’s supporters say they’re voting for him, while 46% say it’s mainly against Cooper. By contrast, 84% of Cooper supporters say they’re voting for him rather than against Whatley (13%).
FOX NEWS POLL: SIGNIFICANT SUPPORT FOR BOTH VOTER ID LAWS AND MAIL-IN BALLOTS

Most voters are committed to their choice: 81% of Cooper’s backers say they’re certain to vote for him and it’s 77% among Whatley supporters. Overall, one in five voters say they could switch their pick.

President Trump complicates the contest for Whatley. Forty percent of North Carolina voters view the president favorably and 58% unfavorable. That’s net negative by 18 points, while his ratings were underwater by just 6 points two years ago (47-53%).

And Whatley’s ties to Trump concern 48% of voters, with worry extending across the spectrum, including more than half of moderates, more than 4 in 10 independents, and about 3 in 10 non-MAGA Republicans. Meanwhile, concern about Cooper’s ties to the Democratic establishment is more partisan. Overall, 42% are concerned, including 7 in 10 Republicans, but just 3 in 10 independents and moderates.

"Recent data put the average Republican advantage in North Carolina statewide races at about 3 points," says Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the survey with Democrat Chris Anderson. "Cooper’s edge rests on almost unanimous Democratic support and commanding numbers among independents. To win, Whatley must stop the bleeding with non-MAGA Republicans and improve his standing with disaffected, less partisan Carolinians."

Personal popularity also sets the candidates apart. Cooper’s 54% favorable rating is significantly higher than Whatley’s at 40%. In addition, Cooper is more popular than the Democratic Party by a 12-point margin, while Whatley trails the GOP by 4.
Whatley is less well known overall, as 14% of voters say they’re unable to rate him or have never heard of him, including about 1 in 10 Republicans.
Tar Heel voters share equally negative views of the Republican Party (44% favorable vs. 54% unfavorable) and the Democratic Party (42% vs. 56%).

Negative partisanship is strong, as more Democrats view the GOP negatively (94%) than view their own party positively (83%). The reverse is also true: more Republicans (92%) hold an unfavorable opinion of the Democratic Party than view the GOP positively (85%).
Among the small subgroup viewing both parties negatively, Cooper draws twice as much support as Whatley (64% to 32%).

Inflation is the top issue for North Carolina voters, with 36% saying it will be most important to their vote for Senate. Next, it’s political divisions within the country at 14%, followed closely by healthcare and immigration at 13% each.
CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE
Half describe their financial situation as stable, 12% say they’re getting ahead, and 38% say they’re falling behind, which is 6 points lower than it was two years ago.

North Carolina’s recent voting history points in different directions. Cooper won reelection in 2020 by almost 5 percentage points. In fact, Democrats have won 8 of the state’s last 10 gubernatorial elections. The last Republican to win was Pat McCrory, by about 11 points in 2012.
At the same time, Republicans have won the state in 11 of the last 12 presidential elections. The last Democrat to carry the state was former President Obama, who won by 0.3% in 2008.
In the 2024 presidential election, Trump won North Carolina by 3 percentage points.

Conducted July 23-27, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 1,005 North Carolina registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file.  Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (115) and cellphones (654) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (236). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ± 3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Sources used to develop weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis, and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education, and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population.  Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100.
Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.
As head of the polling unit, Dana Blanton runs the Fox News Poll and oversees the Fox News Voter Analysis election survey.

title: Fetterman brands new socialist favorite 'Pontiac Platner' after 'ogre' dig
summary: John Fetterman branded Michigan Senate candidate Abdulrahman El-Sayed "Pontiac Platner" and accused him of leading the party's "pro-Hamas wing."
story: Democratic strategist Al Mottur and former U.S. Senate candidate Tiffany Smiley discuss the backlash against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed after he referred to Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., as an 'ogre on a pike' during a donor call.

Senator John Fetterman, D-Pa., branded Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdulrahman El-Sayed "Pontiac Platner" after the left-wing upstart called for the "ogre" to be put on a "pike" at a campaign event in comments widely understood to reference the Pennsylvania lawmaker.

A recording from a Zoom call with donors obtained by Politico appeared to depict El-Sayed railing against those who have criticized his far-left policy platform, while singling out Fetterman and allegedly envisioning his head on a stake.
Fetterman later responded to CNBC’s Joe Kernen by blessing El-Sayed with a new nickname.

"I never worked out in male modeling. You know, you could call me ‘Senator Shrek’ — whatever — but this guy is really the Pontiac Platner, and now he’s really running to be, be the head of our emerging pro-Hamas wing here in the party," Fetterman said of El-Sayed.
DEM SENATE HOPEFUL UNDER FIRE FOR RESURFACED COMMENTS CALLING COPS 'OPPORTUNISTIC COWARDS'
U.S. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., speaks to reporters outside the Senate chamber during votes Nov. 10, 2025, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Pontiac is a well-known name in Michigan, stemming from the 18th century Odawa chief to his namesake city and the now-defunct General Motors brand that was discontinued following the 2008 financial crisis.

El-Sayed has routinely criticized the Israeli government, and some of his policy positions overlap with those of Maine oyster farmer Graham Platner, who dropped his Senate bid after a series of allegations of sexual misconduct involving women.
"Politically, some of the things that he said or done are unacceptable to me. I'm not really sure what I've really done or voted for that that has offended the little guy so much," Fetterman added.
BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images; Sarah Rice/Getty Images)
He added that Democrats are engaging in a "serious game" by allowing people in the "Bernie Sanders" wing of the party who "created the Platner disaster" some policy oxygen.
During El-Sayed’s Zoom call, the millennial left-winger spoke out specifically against Fetterman.

"In the interim need to be organizing downward and outward. So, a big pickup for us could be that John Fetterman seat [in Pennsylvania]. I’m like a lot of folks — they’re going to ‘F’ around and give me carte blanche to go take them out," El-Sayed said.
"Y’all came at me, so now I get to come at you and primary people like John Fetterman, and I have no problem with that. I'm looking forward to it."

El-Sayed dismissed the longstanding custom against primarying sitting senators, a norm recently broken in the GOP when Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton defeated incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn in their primary.
"Then, what happens is, ideally, you put one ogre on a pike, and then everyone else gets the message and all of a sudden starts to sound a lot different," El-Sayed said.

The 6-foot-9 Fetterman took the insult in stride in his interview with Kernen, alluding to El-Sayed’s barb being his latest comparison to Mike Myers’ beloved green ogre that has cropped up in memes and elsewhere over the years.

"It's incumbent on us, Republican and Democrat [alike], to police your own ranks. So, that's what I'm willing to do," Fetterman said, adding he is warning fellow lawmakers against eliminating the filibuster in one example.

El-Sayed and Platner also share several policy positions, including support for a single-payer, government-run Medicare-for-all system, anti-corporate housing policies, higher taxes on wealthy Americans and alignment with Sanders, a Vermont socialist.
While El-Sayed says he is neither a Democratic Socialists of America member nor a democratic socialist, he has a history of speaking at DSA events.

Between 2017 and 2020, El-Sayed attended and spoke at six events held by the DSA, including a 2019 fundraiser he headlined. Despite the longstanding relationship, El-Sayed has distanced himself from the DSA when interviewed by the press and outright rejected being labeled a "socialist."

summary: DHS general counsel James Percival blasted the "liberal media" after a reporter questioned whether his series criticizing activist judges risks threats.

GOP SENATOR UNVEILS BOASBERG ACT TO STOP 'ROGUE' JUDGES FROM HANDPICKING TRUMP CASES

After his posts, Percival said DHS was contacted by a Chicago Sun-Times reporter about whether "a social media post like this risk[s] additional threats" in the context of "ongoing threats to federal judges."

ICE agents knock on the door of a residence during a multi-agency targeted enforcement operation in Chicago Jan. 26, 2025. (Bloomberg)

JUSTICE NEIL GORSUCH BREAKS SILENCE ON VIOLENT THREATS AGAINST JUDICIARY, SUPREME COURT LEAKS
