title: Schumer dodges question on whether DSA belongs in Democratic Party
summary: Chuck Schumer dodged a question about whether the Democratic Socialists of America platform belongs in the Democratic Party amid socialist primary wins.
story: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., declined to answer whether the DSA platform’s call to abolish the Senate has a place in the Democratic Party.
As the Democratic Party's socialist wing racks up primary victories, one top Democrat is emphasizing that the party remains a big tent.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., dodged a question from Fox News on Wednesday about whether the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) platform has a place in the Democratic Party.

"[The] bottom line is Democrats from one end of the spectrum to the other are going to be working to defeat Trump, to bring down costs, to go after his corruption and to end the chaos," Schumer replied at a leadership news conference.
The Senate minority leader did not elaborate on whether he agreed with the DSA’s call to abolish the Senate.

Senate Minority Leader, Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference following a weekly policy luncheon with Senate Democrats at the U.S. Capitol on June 2, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
WATCH: HOUSE DEMS DODGE QUESTIONS ON SOCIALIST AGENDA THAT THREATENS TO ABOLISH KEY INSTITUTIONS
The Senate has frequently drawn criticism from socialists for giving equal power to all states and its 60-vote threshold requiring bipartisan consensus to pass most legislation.

The Senate abolition proposal is part of the DSA's recent platform, "Workers Deserve More," which also calls for scrapping the presidency and the Supreme Court in favor of representatives "chosen by" and "subordinate to" a unicameral Congress.
In the manifesto, the far-left group also calls for abolishing the police and prisons, defunding the Department of War, and dismantling capitalism.
The exchange comes as Schumer’s path to political power is increasingly colliding with the socialist movement's growing strength.

After upsetting Democratic incumbents in New York City and Colorado this year, the DSA is attempting to keep its winning streak alive by electing more socialist candidates in upcoming primaries in Missouri and Michigan.

If Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed, a far-left candidate who has rejected the "socialist" label, wins the hotly contested Democratic primary, Schumer’s hopes of becoming Senate majority leader could depend on his victory in November.
The New York Democrat has thrown his support behind Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., who has consolidated support among the party’s establishment wing, in the key Senate race.
Schumer could also face a primary threat from the Democratic Party’s far-left flank if he seeks reelection in 2028.
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed poses for a portrait in Grand Rapids, Mich., on Feb. 21, 2026. (Evan Cobb for The Washington Post via Getty Images)
DSA MEMBER LEADS DEM PRIMARY IN MIDWEST BATTLEGROUND BUT TRAILS LIKELY GOP NOMINEE: POLL
Some moderate Democrats have called on the party to take a harder line in rejecting the DSA.
"This isn’t a big tent—it’s anarchy," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., wrote on social media earlier this week. "Why can’t Dems call out the DSA?"
DSA co-chair Megan Romer affirmed the group supports many of these policy ideas during a recent interview with "Fox News Sunday."
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., speaks to reporters outside the Senate chamber during votes on Nov. 10, 2025, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
"[You're advocating for] abolish[ing] the Senate?" Fox News’ Shannon Bream asked.
"True," Romer responded.
"Replace the presidency and Supreme Court as we now know them?" Bream followed up.
"Yep," Romer replied.

"Absolutely," Romer said.
Whether Democratic leaders embrace or distance themselves from the DSA will be a defining question heading into the November midterms.

title: Iran mines US troops' social media as military considers seizing cellphones
summary: Adm. Brad Cooper warned that photos and videos posted online give Iran near-real-time battle-damage assessments that could cost American lives.
story: Retired General Jack Keane discusses President Donald Trump's strong remarks on Iran, asserting that a 'beating' for the regime necessitates a comprehensive attack.

Some U.S. troops deployed to the Middle East may soon be ordered to surrender their cellphones as military leaders warn that Iran is using photos and videos posted online to assess where its strikes landed and potentially improve follow-up attacks, Reuters first reported Wednesday.

Some service members stationed in Jordan have been told their phones will be confiscated in the coming days, two sources familiar with the matter told the outlet. A third source said cellphone restrictions were being considered more broadly across the region because of operational security concerns but did not describe the move as certain.
Any crackdown would force U.S. military commanders to balance operational security against troops’ reliance on cellphones to communicate with their families during wartime.

Some U.S. troops deployed to the Middle East may soon be ordered to surrender their cellphones as military leaders warn that Iran is using photos and videos posted online to assess where its strikes landed and potentially improve follow-up attacks.  (Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images)
TWO US SERVICE MEMBERS KILLED IN IRANIAN STRIKES ON JORDAN, CENTCOM SAYS

U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), the military command that leads U.S. military operations in the Middle East, confirmed to Fox News Digital that commander Adm. Brad Cooper sent the internal message described in the report but declined to release it publicly.

"The message is a general reminder to our service members on the importance of maintaining operational security," CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins said. "This is one of many opportunities Admiral Cooper has used to convey operational priorities."

A defense official declined to tell Fox News Digital whether personnel had been ordered to surrender their phones or whether wider restrictions were under consideration, saying CENTCOM does not discuss force-protection tactics and techniques for operational security reasons.
SECRET SERVICE AGENT ON JD VANCE'S DETAIL INVESTIGATED FOR ALLEGEDLY LEAKING OPERATIONAL SECURITY INFO
The message warned that online posts were giving Iran near-real-time information about whether its missile and drone attacks had succeeded, according to Reuters, which obtained a copy.
Iran can search news reports and social media for reactions, photos and cellphone footage showing where its weapons landed, Cooper reportedly wrote.
"The direct, unavoidable cost of this open-source intelligence could be measured in the lives of American service members," Cooper warned.
U.S. Central Command confirmed to Fox News Digital that commander Adm. Brad Cooper sent the internal message described in the report but declined to release it publicly. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

Cooper reportedly pointed to footage posted online during the July 17 Iranian attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, which killed Pvt. Isabella Gonzales and fatally wounded 1st Lt. Tyler Feehan. Sgt. Angel Rampersad also is believed to have been killed in the attack.
The footage, captured using a service member’s Meta smart glasses, showed troops running for shelter and where the individual evacuated.

Without such information, Iran could have difficulty determining whether its weapons missed, struck an empty area or hit a populated facility, Cooper wrote. Publicly available details can effectively provide Iran with a battle-damage assessment and help it plan more devastating follow-up attacks, he warned.

Cellphone rules vary widely across the military. Personal devices already are prohibited during some sensitive missions and inside classified areas, while sailors at sea often lack ordinary cellular service. Many troops stationed at established overseas bases, however, often retain use of their phones.

The concern raised in Cooper’s message is distinct from another cellphone-related vulnerability reported by Fox News Digital in June — adversaries’ potential access to commercially available location data generated by smartphones, apps and advertising networks.
CENTCOM told lawmakers it had received "multiple threat reports concerning adversary exploitation of commercial location data to target or surveil U.S. personnel in theater."

A bipartisan group led by Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., subsequently accused the Pentagon of failing to take basic precautions against the threat posed by data brokers, which collect and sell information about users’ movements.

The lawmakers said adversaries could potentially use that information to identify military installations, monitor troop movements or track individual service members. They urged the Pentagon to disable advertising identifiers on government-issued smartphones and direct personnel to take similar precautions on personal devices.

Justin Sherman, CEO of research and advisory firm Global Cyber Strategies, previously told Fox News Digital that foreign adversaries could obtain cellphone location data through brokers, digital advertising networks and other commercial systems.
People stand on a bridge destroyed after a strike in Hormozgan province, southern Iran, July 18, 2026. (Amirhosein Khorgooi/Iranian Students' News Agency via AP)
"The sale of location data, in particular on Americans’ devices, puts military personnel at risk," Sherman said, calling it "a serious national security threat."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

While the earlier warning focused on information collected and sold by commercial companies, Cooper’s message addressed material posted publicly, including footage that can reveal where troops sought shelter and whether Iranian strikes hit their intended targets.
The Pentagon referred Fox News Digital to CENTCOM when asked for comment. Iran's Mission to the United Nations in New York could not immediately be reached for comment.

title: Trump unveils gleaming gold makeover of iconic DC horse statues
summary: President Trump shared photos as crews dismantle scaffolding around the Arts of War sculptures' restored golden horses near Arlington Memorial Bridge.
story: Crews unveiled the newly regilded Arts of War statues near the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C. after months of restoration.

President Donald Trump offered Americans a first look at the newly regilded Arts of War sculptures in Washington, D.C., as crews began removing the towering scaffolding that concealed the iconic golden horses during months of restoration work.

"Taking down the scaffolding around the regilded Arts of War sculptures!" Trump wrote on Truth Social, sharing photographs of workers carefully dismantling the structure surrounding the massive monument near the Lincoln Memorial.
Exclusive Fox News video captured workers removing the final sections of scaffolding, revealing the gleaming gold horses and figures that crown the monumental granite pedestals.

The Arts of War sculptures flank the eastern entrance to Arlington Memorial Bridge just west of the Lincoln Memorial, while their companion Arts of Peace sculptures sit nearby along Parkway Drive. Each monument features gilded bronze horses and human figures mounted atop massive granite bases, according to a study by MTFA Design.
TOP TRUMP OFFICIAL TOUTS HOW DC MAKEOVER IS PROOF AMERICA IS REJECTING 'DECLINE BY CHOICE'

A worker stands between the newly regilded legs of an Arts of War horse statue as scaffolding is removed during restoration work near the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., in this image shared by President Donald Trump on Truth Social. (President Donald Trump/Truth Social)

The restoration is part of an ongoing National Park Service preservation project. According to the same 2018 study, the granite pedestals had developed extensive purple staining caused by copper runoff from the aging bronze sculptures, prompting specialized cleaning and stabilization work in addition to regilding.

The agency temporarily closed surrounding lawn and turf areas beginning July 2 to protect visitors, workers and the historic monuments while construction continues. The restrictions are scheduled to remain in effect through Sept. 30, though the National Park Service said areas will reopen as soon as the work no longer requires them to remain closed.
‘DERANGED’ VANDALS FUEL MALL SABOTAGE TREND, FROM BLOOD WRITING TO REFLECTING POOL DAMAGE

Workers dismantle scaffolding surrounding a newly regilded Arts of War horse statue near Arlington Memorial Bridge in Washington, D.C., in this image shared by President Donald Trump on Truth Social. (President Donald Trump/Truth Social)
Sidewalks bordering the restoration area and those leading onto Memorial Bridge remain accessible, and the project has not required any road closures, according to the agency.
The surrounding parkland will remain partially restricted while crews complete the broader rehabilitation project and remove the remaining construction equipment.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Scaffolding remains around a newly regilded Arts of War statue during ongoing restoration work near the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., in this image shared by President Donald Trump on Truth Social. (President Donald Trump/Truth Social)
For months, the towering monuments were almost entirely hidden behind scaffolding, tarps and fencing.
Trump's photos and Fox News' exclusive video now offer one of the clearest looks yet at the restored sculptures are unveiled with a renewed gold finish just in time for America's 250th anniversary.
The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: WATCH: Fetterman reveals his ‘one regret’ from COVID era after Fauci testimony

story: Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., spoke with Fox News Digital after attending the Senate hearing with Dr. Anthony Fauci, sharing he wishes he'd been more willing to consider the COVID lab leak theory. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

title: Senator’s F-bomb bashing of Fauci rocks Internet: ‘High-heat fastball!’
summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno dropped an F-bomb at Anthony Fauci during the congressional hearing as the former COVID-19 advisor invoked the Fifth Amendment.
story: Sen. Bernie Moreno teared into Anthony Fauci for his COVID-19 policies, accusing Fauci of being interested in meeting with celebrities than administering to the American people.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, tore into Dr. Anthony Fauci, who served as President Joe Biden's chief medical advisor and was a key government spokesman during the COVID-19 pandemic, dropping an F-bomb during Wednesday's congressional hearing.

Fauci was issued a subpoena by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., as part of a congressional investigation into the origins of COVID-19 and the federal government's response to the pandemic. Paul, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and his Republican colleagues have long accused Fauci of misleading Congress and the American people about the origins of the virus, federal funding for research at the Wuhan Institute of Virology in the Chinese city where the virus first emerged and the nature of so-called gain-of-function research, which alters pathogens to study how they may become more transmissible or dangerous.
"Here I am sitting in front of you six years later saying, who the f--k do you think you were for doing that?" Moreno said. "It is a total disgrace what you did to this country."
FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL
A split image shows Anthony Fauci and Sen. Bernie Moreno (Allison Robbert / AP)

Moreno's remarks came after he argued the government's COVID-19 guidance, including mask mandates, social distancing recommendations and school closures, harmed Americans. He said "moronic" politicians' implementation of Fauci's guidance led to arrests, recounting the story of an Ohio mother who was arrested for not wearing a mask during an outdoor high school football game.

"When that story broke, I said to myself, I cannot stand idly on the side and watch this happen," Moreno said. "It was about six years ago today that I decided I'm going to give up my businesses, sell them all, run for office, run for the United States Senate."

Moreno then asked Fauci whether he would apologize to the American people, prompting Fauci to invoke the Fifth Amendment. Throughout the hearing, Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment more than 100 times rather than answer lawmakers' questions.

Fauci served as chief medical adviser to President Donald Trump during the COVID-19 pandemic before later continuing in the role under President Joe Biden. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Moreno accused Fauci of being more interested in rubbing elbows with celebrities such as Kim Kardashian, referring to a Zoom call Fauci participated in with her and more than a dozen other celebrities, than serving as a public health official.

title: Top 5 moments from Fauci's hearing: Paul boots lawyer, Moreno erupts as contempt vote looms
summary: Anthony Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment 111 times during Rand Paul's Senate hearing, refusing to answer questions about gain-of-function research.
story: Dr. Anthony Fauci and Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., were finally set to hash out their feud, but the hearing quickly derailed when Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment, his lawyer was booted, and a senator exploded in frustration.

What was billed as a battle of wits between Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and Dr. Anthony Fauci, with the lawmaker determined to uncover the former COVID-19 explainer-in-chief’s motivations during the pandemic, became a one-sided affair in the Senate.

Paul has for years sought to uncover Fauci’s alleged role in funding "risky" research in China that Republicans say sparked the pandemic in 2020. He has argued that Fauci should be thrown in prison, and that the former chief medical advisor to the president’s pardon from former President Joe Biden wouldn’t hold up.
But the highly anticipated back and forth, which was further stoked by Paul dumping over 1,000 pages of Fauci’s diary online before the hearing, didn’t go exactly as planned.

The hearing kicked off with an impassioned opening statement from Paul, who accused Fauci and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) of funding gain-of-function research for years, misleading Congress and destroying records, which he contended created a fracture in public trust over the nation’s COVID-19 response.

"That loss of trust may be your most damaging legacy," Paul said. "Trust can't be ordered. It has to be earned. No scientist is above scrutiny. No government official beyond accountability, and no public servant preferred version of history."
RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES
But Fauci, under guidance from his lawyers, opted against answering any questions from Paul or others on the committee.

He argued that Paul's "obvious obsession" with pushing for his prosecution, levying allegations against him, and dumping his unredacted diary was designed to "get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, quote, behind bars, unquote."

"Although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government, and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions," Fauci said.
It wasn’t long after Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment that tensions flared in the hearing.
After being repeatedly asked questions, and repeatedly turning to his constitutional shield, Paul declared that as chair of the committee, he was denying Fauci’s right to invoke the Fifth Amendment.
"It's against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress," Paul said. "There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today."
WATCH: RAND PAUL SAYS THERE'S ONE THING AMERICANS HAVE NEVER HEARD FROM FAUCI
Then Fauci’s lawyer, David Schertler, spoke up to remind Paul it was Fauci’s constitutional right to turn to the Fifth Amendment.

Paul reminded Schertler that neither he, nor the "half dozen" lawyers with Fauci were recognized by the committee. That prompted Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., the top Democrat on the panel, to push for Schertler to speak.
But Paul was not having it.

"This is the way Anthony Fauci wants to be remembered — for a lawyer not listening to the rules," Paul said. "That's the way you want to be remembered, and that's what you're going to do. You are not recognized, sir. Security, please remove him from the room."
The hearing chugged along at roughly the same pace — lawmakers would ask Fauci a question, then he would invoke the Fifth Amendment.
But that didn’t stop some on the panel from getting frustrated at his lack of forthrightness.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, noted that Schertler was a well-known lawyer who previously represented former Sen. Bob Menendez, who was sentenced for accepting gold bars and bribes in exchange for using his influence to benefit the Egyptian government.
WATCH: RAND PAUL SAYS FAUCI LOBBIED FOR $1M PRIZE WHILE LEADING COVID RESPONSE

"And there's an article here in the Washington Free Beacon that talks about why you would hire a guy like David Schertler. And the comment is, if you're in deep s---, that's who you call," Moreno said. "Do you feel like you're in deep s---?"

Fauci again declined to answer, which prompted a frustrated Moreno to tell him that his influence over policy during the pandemic in 2020 and the effect that it had on Americans pushed him to run for the Senate.
"Here I am sitting in front of you six years later saying, ‘Who the f— do you think you were for doing that? It is a total disgrace what you did to this country,’" Moreno said.
As the hearing wound down, Paul revisited his threat to hold Fauci accountable for declining to answer questions.
Paul announced that he would seek contempt charges against Fauci after he invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination and teed up a vote in committee for next week.

"We're going to have a vote next week on contempt," Paul said. "I think there's another legal question that the courts may have to decide upon, and that is whether or not a presidential pardon offers you complete immunity."
Dr. Anthony Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right to remain silent over 100 times during Wednesday's hearing. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Fauci never answered a question from any lawmaker on either side of the aisle, sticking to the advice from his lawyers to invoke the Fifth Amendment to protect himself from self-incrimination.
Before the hearing started, Paul and his staff were confident that Fauci wouldn't try to invoke the Fifth Amendment.

So confident, a source familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital, that several questions were prepared ahead of time, and members of the committee were told to come prepared.

title: Top union 'cleared' by law firm over explosive corruption allegation previously gave millions to that firm
summary: Pitta LLP received $11.6 million from the Hotel Trades Council and Unite Here Local 6 while investigating whistleblower corruption claims against them.
story: Vice President JD Vance and some House Republicans are pushing union-friendly legislation, signaling a new era for the Republican party. Paul Gigot discusses the Railway Safety Act and mandatory arbitration for labor contracts, viewed as creating union jobs without enhancing safety. Critics suggest this strategy targets blue-collar workers and Teamsters endorsement for 2028, raising concerns about economic impacts and deregulation.

A law firm that says it found no evidence to support corruption allegations against two New York City unions has long-running financial and familial ties to those labor organizations, public records show.

The Hotel Trades Council (HTC) and UNITE HERE Local 6 (UH6) hired Pitta LLP to investigate a whistleblower letter alleging a culture of quid pro quo corruption and improper gift-giving at the two unions. The firm’s review was completed in March 2026. While Pitta LLP ultimately found no evidence that the two labor organizations had broken the law, the firm had previously received millions from the unions. The firm's leaders also share family ties with former union leaders.
Some legal experts said this could lead to an appearance of impropriety.
Though the financial and familial relationships may raise eyebrows, Pitta LLP had no legal obligation to disclose them in its review.
SOURCES CORROBORATE WHISTLEBLOWER CLAIMS OF CORRUPTION, QUID PRO QUO CULTURE INSIDE POWERFUL NYC UNION

President Rich Maroko speaks during a press conference with New York Mayoral Candidate Zohran Mamdani at the Hotel & Gaming Trades Council building on July 2, 2025, in New York City. Mamdani celebrated his mayoral primary victory with leaders and members of the city’s labor unions, including the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, 32BJ SEIU, New York State Nurses Association, and NY City Central Labor Council, and received the endorsements of these unions.  (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

Between 2020 and 2025, HTC and UH6 collectively paid $11.6 million to Pitta LLP for legal services, an average of nearly $2 million a year, according to disclosure documents filed with the department.

The Center for Union Facts (CUF), a nonprofit watchdog group that is sharply critical of labor unions and union leadership, provided documentation to Fox News Digital showing that the father of Vincent Pitta, the law firm’s chairman, held leadership positions at the two unions and that his sister is married to Peter Ward, HTC’s former president. Pitta later confirmed both relationships in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital obtained and reviewed the preliminary statement from a second independent investigation conducted by a former state and federal prosecutor affiliated with a different law firm that also concluded that there was no evidence to support any of the allegations of misconduct set forth in the whistleblower letter.

"When confronted with information suggesting that employees, consultants, or other business partners have engaged in serious misconduct, most companies’ first reaction is to consult with a trusted outside firm with which the company has a long working relationship," the law firm Quinn Emanuel wrote in a 2022 publication. "But there are drawbacks to this approach. In a complex internal investigation, a company’s longtime corporate counsel can become subject to ethical conflicts, confirmation bias, divergent incentives and other issues that may produce a suboptimal result for the client."
Quinn Emanuel’s blog post relates to general legal ethics, not the facts of the relationship between Pitta LLP and the two labor unions.

"Companies facing potential criminal or regulatory investigations or any allegation of serious misconduct almost always will be better served by hiring counsel that does not have a long history of providing corporate or transactional advice to the company," the publication continued. "Even where the firm’s lawyers can acknowledge, for example, misconduct by the executives from whom the lawyers have taken instructions, confronting those issues creates tricky reputational and financial problems for the firm … the firm might fear that the company’s board of directors or other executives not implicated in misconduct will blame the firm, thereby jeopardizing the firm’s relationship with the company going forward."
UNIONS THAT PARALYZED NEW YORK COMMUTE OVER PAY SPENT MILLIONS ON LUXURY TRAVEL, FILINGS SHOW
A State of Emergency was declared for New York City. (Nikolas Lanum/Fox News Digital)

The American College of Trial Lawyers, similarly, released guidance for internal investigations in 2020 which noted that government prosecutors "might be skeptical of an internal investigation of high-level or sensitive wrongdoing conducted by outside counsel regularly retained by the company" because "regular counsel may have a motive to avoid criticizing, and thus alienating, senior management, the source of past and future law firm revenues."

McKenna Long & Aldridge, another law firm, noted that engaging a firm with which an entity has "significant economic ties" presents "an obvious risk to independence" that must be weighed against the benefit provided by their familiarity with the case.
Pitta, in a statement to Fox News Digital, denied that financial and familial ties presented a conflict of interest when investigating the claims made against HTC and UH6.

"Our four-decade relationship with the unions, did not and does not constitute a conflict of interest as it relates to the expedited preliminary review conducted by one of our partners of the ‘anonymous allegations’ which you are interested in," he wrote. "We assiduously ‘call them, as we see them,’ to steal some baseball vernacular — without fear or favor."
Pitta said his firm charges the two unions a reasonable rate for its legal services.

"If the $12 million figure is accurate," he said, the average cost spread across the roughly 40,000 members of the unions would come out to just around "$1 per member per week for expert labor, employment, employee benefits, election law, and other requested legal services."

Sam Levine, commissioner of the New York Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, from left, Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, and Rich Maroko, president of the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council (HTC), during an announcement on junk fees in the Susan and John Hess Family Theater at The Whitney Museum of American Art in New York, on Wednesday, Jan. 21, 2026. Mamdani announced rules that banned hotels from charging consumers hidden junk fees.   (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
UTAH JUSTICE ALLEGEDLY SENT ‘INAPPROPRIATE’ TEXTS TO LAWYER IN KEY REDISTRICTING CASE, OFFICIALS LAUNCH PROBE

He also confirmed that his father, who passed away in 2005, held leadership positions at the two unions for roughly 30 years and that his sister is married to Ward. Pitta maintains that neither relationship constituted a conflict of interest and that, if it did, the firm would address it with the "highest ethical standards and the best practices of our profession."
Critics of organized labor, however, see things differently.
"Tapping the union's family firm doesn't exactly inspire confidence in the results," CUF communications director Charlyce Bozzello told Fox News Digital.
CUF has repeatedly targeted Richard Maroko, who serves as president of UH6 and HTC.

"The contract with Pitta originated under the previous administration and there have been no familial relationships with the union for more than 6 years," HTC spokesman Austin Shafran told Fox News Digital. "During that time, the firm has handled over 1000 arbitration cases for the union, recovering more than $200 million that went directly into the pockets of our members."

Sources familiar with the inner workings of UH6 and HTC previously told Fox News Digital that leadership at the two unions had what they described as an unusually close relationship with hotel management — a relationship they alleged allowed hotel owners to strike beneficial deals in exchange for information that helped union leaders retain their power.
The sources further alleged that individuals involved in hotel management provided union leaders with improper gifts, such as high-end food and drink, to build relationships with them.

An HTC spokesman previously flatly denied the underlying whistleblower claims, pointing to two investigations the union commissioned, including Pitta LLP’s March 2026 review, which found no evidence to support claims that hotel management was unusually close to union leadership or that union officials accepted improper gifts.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Two exhaustive, independent investigations, including one by a former federal prosecutor, have concluded that these anonymous claims are frivolous, lack any factual basis, and were clearly an attempt to derail contract negotiations between the union and hotel management," HTC spokesman Austin Shafran previously told Fox News Digital. "Thankfully, these efforts failed as our union secured the best contract in its history that will provide unprecedented wage increases and benefits to tens of thousands of hotel workers. Nothing will ever deter the union from working every day to better the lives of our members and their families."

No HTC or UH6 leader, and no hotel executive allegedly involved in the whistleblower claims, has been charged with a crime or found to have engaged in professional misconduct in connection with the allegations.

title: Former Democratic staffers, DEI leaders shape Smithsonian leadership amid political firestorm
summary: A Fox News Digital review of biographies and social media profiles identified roughly two dozen people employed by the Smithsonian with ties to the left.
story: Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas., joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss Republican lawmakers' claims that the Smithsonian Museum is using its exhibits for left-wing activism instead of history.

As Republicans intensify scrutiny of the Smithsonian Institution, numerous former Democratic staffers and employees of progressive nonprofits are holding senior positions throughout the nonprofit, while officials responsible for hiring emphasized diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives.

A Fox News Digital review of public biographies and social media profiles identified roughly two dozen individuals employed by the Smithsonian in leadership positions or as curators who worked for Democratic offices or progressive nonprofits before being hired. Leadership biographies and political donation records indicate the pattern extends beyond a handful of senior employees.

That former Democratic staffers and individuals previously employed by liberal nonprofits now hold leadership positions at the Smithsonian is likely to further fuel conservative criticism that the sprawling museum and research organization has developed a left-of-center bias.
TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

As Republicans intensify scrutiny of the Smithsonian Institution, numerous former Democratic staffers and employees of progressive nonprofits hold senior positions throughout the nonprofit. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)

In recent weeks, Republicans have accused the Smithsonian, particularly its National Museum of American History, of promoting progressive ideology, emphasizing identity politics and giving insufficient attention to the nation’s founding and traditional historical figures. Republican lawmakers and the Trump administration also have criticized specific exhibits addressing gender identity, diversity and social justice, arguing that museum leaders have allowed political activism to displace the neutral presentation of history.
These allegations follow years of DEI-centric leadership.

Roshni Lal, the director of the Smithsonian’s office of academic appointments and internships, which oversees academic hiring and internships, has had a career-long commitment to advancing DEI in hiring, professional biographies show.

Lal previously was the director of diversity, equity and inclusion for the Mountain Pacific Association of Colleges & Employers, where she oversaw policies, training and programming she characterized as anti-racist and rooted in social justice, according to her Smithsonian biography. She also held DEI-related roles at the Manhattan Beach Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Colleges and Employers before joining the Smithsonian, per Lal’s LinkedIn page.
In a 2024 podcast appearance, Lal discussed her dedication to "identity-based career services," partially through connecting with "students of color" through "culturally inclusive" job placement.

Public Smithsonian biographies show that several curators at the National Museum of American History describe their work as focusing on race, identity and social justice, themes that also appear in a number of the museum's exhibits and initiatives.
WATCH: ‘SHOCKING’ BEN FRANKLIN SMEAR LEAVES SMITHSONIAN CHIEF WITH ‘NO REGRETS’

The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History is being called out for being "ideologically captured" and presenting woke revisionist history on the weekend of America's 250th birthday. (Kevin Carter)

The current chairwoman of the National Museum of American History political history division, which is responsible for overseeing exhibits about American presidents, for instance, also oversees the Smithsonian’s Center for Restorative History, which says on its website that it exists to "spotlight the people and stories that have been excluded from our national narrative using the principles of restorative justice" by bringing together "diverse voices."

Among the center’s flagship programs are an effort to preserve the history of the Black Lives Matter movement by centering the perspectives of activists and a "decolonization working group," according to its website.

Multiple other curators at the National Museum of American History approach their jobs with a similar focus on racial identity, per their Smithsonian biographies. These include one curator who is working on "stitching social justice throughout the Americas" through their exhibit work as well as multiple scholars who primarily study race.

While Lal started her role at the Smithsonian in November 2023, her predecessor, who held the position for 11 years beginning in 2012, previously worked for the Clinton White House, the Obama State Department and as a special assistant to then-Sen. Hillary Clinton, according to his LinkedIn profile.
Lal did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital Tuesday.

"The Smithsonian is a nonpartisan institution, and politics does not factor into our hiring practices," a spokesperson for the institution told Fox News Digital. "Our hiring is solely based on qualifications to fulfill the responsibilities of any given position."

Leadership at the Smithsonian is not monolithic. The institution’s chief legal officer worked in the Bush administration, and the chief of staff to the organization's regents clerked for Chief Justice John G. Roberts on the Supreme Court as well as Justice Brett Kavanaugh during his time on D.C.'s federal appellate court, according to their institutional biographies.
DEI HIRING BOOST FOR ONE BLUE STATE'S MUSLIM COMMISSION INITIATIVE FLIES IN FACE OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WOKE PUSH
The Smithsonian National Museum of American History, which is closed due to the federal government shutdown, in Washington, D.C., Oct. 12, 2025.  (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Congressional Republicans held two hearings to investigate allegations that the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History has used taxpayer money to promote left-wing narratives about race, gender and oppression while minimizing the nation’s founding ideals and achievements. Following the hearings, conservative lawmakers are expected to be using Congress’ spending authority in an attempt to restrict Smithsonian funding to pressure it to remove exhibits they feel are inappropriate.

"These leaders have commandeered an institution that the nation entrusted to them to ensure the transmission and, thus, continuance of American culture and heritage and have perversely turned it into its opposite, a hothouse for anti-American activism," Heritage Foundation senior fellow Mike Gonzalez said during his July 21 congressional testimony on the Smithsonian.

"These leaders often reveal, in their own words, that they see the world in terms of power dynamics — who has dominance and how to wrest it from them by dismantling the American narrative, all deeply Marxist and Gramscian constructs."

Other senior Smithsonian staffers who came from left-of-center backgrounds, according to LinkedIn profiles and other online biographies, include the National Museum of American History head librarian, who previously worked for the liberal Urban Institute; an advisory board member who was a senior staffer for the late Sen. Dianne Feinstein; the institution’s undersecretary for education, who served as the deputy assistant secretary of education during the Obama administration; the Smithsonian’s associate director of advancement for strategic initiatives, who came from the NAACP; and the director of communications for the National Museum of American History, who worked as a senior staffer for House Democratic leadership before joining the institution.

Curators with liberal backgrounds, per LinkedIn profiles and online biographies, meanwhile, include the recently departed director of curatorial affairs at the National Portrait Gallery, who held multiple DEI-related positions at colleges; an associate curator at the National Museum of the American Indian who was involved with a militant civil rights organization in the 1970s, the American Indian Movement; and a curator of time-based media for the Smithsonian American Art Museum who previously worked for a feminist art gallery.

Fox News Digital considered groups that publicly align with the Democratic Party or those that focus on issues such as environmentalism, racial justice or left-of-center economic policy as liberal for the purposes of its review.

The Smithsonian has roughly 6,400 full-time employees with varying degrees of public documentation. Fox News Digital's review covered a relatively small slice of that total, focusing on publicly identified leadership at the top of the institution as well as leaders at the National Museum of American History and individuals identifying themselves as curators on LinkedIn.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While a full accounting of the political beliefs of the Smithsonian’s senior staff and curators is impossible to glean from public records alone, political donations can provide some insight.

Only about 1% of donations made by individuals identifying themselves as Smithsonian employees have gone to Republican committees this cycle, according to campaign finance records reviewed by Fox News Digital.
Fox News Digital reached each Smithsonian employee mentioned for comment.

title: House progressives revive Green New Deal for public schools as Dem civil war empowers far left
summary: Rep. Pramila Jayapal is leading progressives in introducing a Green New Deal for public schools, legislation that has little chance of passing.
story: The New York Post reveals the Democratic Socialists of America are plotting a radical takeover of New York City public schools. Fox News Digital columnist David Marcus explains DSA's objective to educate children in a 'democratic socialist frame,' teaching the 'Godfathers of Communism' Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels.
The environmental and social justice movement behind the Green New Deal is back at the forefront of Democrats' agenda, this time targeting America's education system.
A group of House progressives led by Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., introduced a bill this week to "establish a Green New Deal for public schools."

"The best way to prepare the next generation is by strengthening core academics, not expanding ideological programs. Parents and taxpayers have every right to expect schools to stay focused on education," Walberg said.
The resurgence of a Green New Deal push by progressives comes amid a growing civil war within the Democratic Party.
Self-proclaimed democratic socialists and candidates affiliated with them are challenging — and in some cases defeating — establishment Democrats in primaries across the country.

title: Reporter's Notebook: Rand Paul's contempt vote crusade could be doomed despite Fauci pleading Fifth 111 times
summary: Rand Paul plans a committee vote to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he invoked the Fifth Amendment 111 times during testimony.
story: Chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram joins 'The Faulkner Focus' to discuss the Senate hearing of Dr. Anthony Fauci and the removal of his attorney.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., will schedule a committee vote next week to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after invoking the Fifth Amendment 111 times today.The committee could vote to hold Fauci in contempt. But it doesn’t stop there.
Contempt of Congress must go before the entire Senate. It takes a simple majority to hold someone in contempt. But such a resolution must clear one filibuster, requiring 60 yeas.
WATCH: FAUCI ATTORNEY EJECTED FROM SENATE HEARING AFTER CHAOTIC EXCHANGE: 'YOU ARE NOT RECOGNIZED!'

Dr. Anthony Fauci, former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, arrives to testify before the House Oversight and Accountability Committee Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic at the Rayburn House Office Building on June 3, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
So, it’s doubtful Fauci is held in contempt.
Even if the Senate broke the filibuster, the Senate must approve a separate resolution to make a criminal referral to Department of Justice.
That would face at least one filibuster, again entailing 60 affirmative votes.

It is more common for the House to hold someone in contempt compared to the Senate. The Senate last successfully held someone in contempt in 1971.
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: Hawley trolls Fauci's blanket Fifth Amendment claims exposing 'contempt for this body'
summary: Anthony Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right dozens of times, refusing to answer even what day it was or what color his tie was at the hearing.
story: Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo, confronts Dr. Anthony Fauci, arguing he has no Fifth Amendment rights due to a pardon.
Former NIAID Director Anthony Fauci’s refusal to answer questions from Congress extended to simple facts, including the day of the week and the color of the tie he was wearing.

Fauci, 85, invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination about as many times as his years alive on Earth, despite Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., asserting that he did not have that right given his current legal status.

Hawley cited a Supreme Court case from 1896, where President Benjamin Harrison’s appointee, Justice Henry Brown, ruled that a witness granted statutory immunity from prosecution could nonetheless be compelled to testify because his immunity displaced pleading the Fifth.
FAUCI PLEADS FIFTH WITH 'ZERO LEGAL JUSTIFICATION' AS CRITICS ERUPT AND DEMAND CONTEMPT CHARGES
In that case, an auditor for a Pittsburgh railroad unsuccessfully challenged a contempt charge for refusing to answer grand jury questions.
Hawley turned to Fauci and tested his repeated Fifth Amendment invocations throughout the hearing, quipping, "Doc, let’s try something."
"What day of the week is it today?" Hawley asked Wednesday.
Fauci replied with his boilerplate invocation of the Fifth Amendment.
"What color tie are you wearing?" Hawley asked.
Fauci declined to answer, again invoking the Fifth Amendment.
‘PRIVILEGED’ HUNTER BIDEN, SPARED BY DAD’S PARDON, BLASTS TRUMP’S CLEMENCY POWER
"Let's just get one thing straight. You don't have any rights under the Fifth Amendment because you've been pardoned, as you very well know," he said, invoking the 1896 Brown v. Walker case.
Hawley, who is also an attorney, added that the legal reality was likely why Fauci’s remaining attorneys were "shifting nervously" behind him.
A top Fauci attorney, David Schertler, had previously been ejected by Paul after refusing to take his assigned seat and remain quiet.
"This isn't about the law. This is about contempt, contempt for this body and contempt for the American people," Hawley said.

"But I think I know why you're doing it. It's because you don't want to answer questions. It's because you did all kinds of terrible things. It's because during the pandemic, you got rich… while people were dying."

Dr. Anthony Fauci testifies before the House Oversight and Accountability Committee Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic at the Rayburn House Office Building in Washington, D.C., on June 3, 2024. The hearing covers findings from a 15-month Republican-led probe into Fauci and the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, followed Hawley with similar questions that Fauci refused to answer.
Moreno said Fauci should know what the Fifth Amendment is if he wanted to invoke it dozens of times.
When he asked Fauci to recite the Fifth Amendment, Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right.
"No, I’m just asking you what it says," Moreno repeated.
"On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution," Fauci said once more.
Moreno then gave a copy of the Constitution to an aide and instructed him to bring it to Fauci to read.
That attempt also prompted the same repeated response from the octogenarian immunologist.
"So you're invoking a right that you don't know who wrote it or what it says? Is that correct?" Moreno quipped.
Fauci again invoked his Fifth Amendment right after declining to recite the amendment when asked.

The attorney for former NIH Director Anthony Fauci (R), David Schertler (L), is removed from the hearing room at the direction of committee chairman Sen. Fox News anchor Harris Faulkner later discussed the legal implications of Fauci's repeated Fifth Amendment invocations.
She cited President Joe Biden’s blanket, retroactive pardon against Fauci, saying that he is "protected from any offenses against the United States he may have taken part in."

Faulkner said the pardon does not cover state criminal prosecutions, future crimes or congressional investigations.
"It does not protect him from prosecution from perjury if he lies under oath after receiving the pardon," she said.

title: Fauci's Fifth Amendment plea shows Biden autopen pardon on 'legally questionable' ground, Comer says
summary: James Comer says Anthony Fauci's autopen pardon is on legally questionable grounds after the former health official pleaded the Fifth more than 100 times.
story: During a heated Senate hearing, Dr. Anthony Fauci invokes his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination. Fauci stated Sen. Rand Paul's "obvious obsession" with prosecuting him, including publicly releasing his unredacted personal diary, led to this decision.

Dr. Anthony Fauci's fight on Capitol Hill may not be over yet, a top House Republican signaled after the former public health official pleaded the Fifth Amendment more than 100 times during an intense Senate hearing on Wednesday.

"If former President Biden’s blanket autopen pardon is valid, then Dr. Fauci has no right to refuse to answer questions," House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., said after the hearing.
"Dr. Fauci clearly knows his autopen pardon is on legally questionable grounds and decided to protect himself today rather than provide the truth to the American people."
FAUCI PLEADS FIFTH WITH 'ZERO LEGAL JUSTIFICATION' AS CRITICS ERUPT AND DEMAND CONTEMPT CHARGES

Then-Chief Medical Advisor to the president, Anthony Fauci, speaks during a briefing on the Omicron COVID-19 variant, watched by then-President Joe Biden in the Roosevelt Room of the White House in Washington, D.C. on Nov. 29, 2021. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)
Fauci appeared before a Senate GOP-led panel on Wednesday amid new scrutiny over how he handled the COVID-19 pandemic, following the release of a diary he kept during the global health crisis.

Comer accused former Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Xavier Becerra of withholding Fauci's diary from the House Oversight Committee during the Biden administration but said Fauci could be facing new questions after its release.

"Based on the release of Dr. Fauci’s diary, which should have been provided to the House Oversight Committee last Congress but was withheld by then-HHS Secretary Becerra, we’ll be asking Dr. Fauci whether he stands by his previous testimony to our Committee. Dr. Fauci’s actions and lies caused irreparable harm to Americans, and he must face accountability," Comer said.
FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

Diary entries made public by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., a longtime Fauci critic and chair of the committee before which Fauci is appearing on Wednesday, showed the high-profile doctor reflecting on his pandemic-era fame and discussing the disease's origins.
Some entries appeared to show Fauci taking credit for influencing policies that closed schools during the pandemic, one of the most hotly debated aspects of how the government handled COVID.
He told the House Oversight Committee in January 2024, however, "I did not close the schools."
EXCLUSIVE: BIDEN PARDON WON'T SHIELD FAUCI IF HE LIES TO CONGRESS, COMER SAYS
Comer warned Fauci ahead of the hearing that the pardon former President Joe Biden issued him in the final hours of his administration would likely not shield him Wednesday.

"Americans are still reaping the consequences of Dr. Fauci's actions. Biden's pardon doesn't cover Dr. Fauci's testimony this week, and if he continues to lie, he must be held accountable," Comer exclusively told Fox News Digital.
Fauci was among several recipients of controversial "preemptive pardons" by Biden at the 11th hour of his White House term.
Rep. James Comer addresses reporters before closed-door testimony in June 2026. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The pardon covers any offenses from January 1, 2014, through its issue date, or any offense related "to his service as Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, as a member of the White House Coronavirus Task Force or the White House COVID-19 Response Team, or as Chief Medical Advisor to the President."
But because the pardon covers conduct during his government service, there will likely be debate over whether it would protect him from liability stemming from his Wednesday testimony.

Paul said his committee would vote on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress next week. A contempt of Congress charge, if found guilty following Justice Department prosecution, would carry a fine of up to $100,000 and a prison sentence of up to one year.

title: Rand Paul seeks contempt charges after Fauci invokes Fifth Amendment more than 100 times
summary: Rand Paul announced he will seek contempt charges after Anthony Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right over 100 times during the hearing.
story: Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo, confronts Dr. Anthony Fauci, arguing he has no Fifth Amendment rights due to a pardon.

Dr. Anthony Fauci, the former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Director, left Wednesday's congressional grilling without answering lawmakers' questions, but Republicans are escalating their fight to compel his testimony.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday that he will seek contempt charges against Fauci after he invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination more than 100 times during the blockbuster hearing.

"We're going to have a vote next week on contempt. I think there's another legal question that the courts may have to decide upon," Paul said. "And that is whether or not a presidential pardon offers you complete immunity."
Chairman Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs confirmation hearing on Jan. 15, 2025, in Washington, D.C.  (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
WATCH: FAUCI ATTORNEY EJECTED FROM SENATE HEARING AFTER CHAOTIC EXCHANGE: ‘YOU ARE NOT RECOGNIZED!’

The move capped off a years-long feud between Paul and Fauci after the senator accused Fauci of lying to Congress about the origins of COVID-19 and funding gain-of-function research in China that he alleged fueled the virus' outbreak.
Paul has previously issued criminal referrals against Fauci and suggested he should face criminal prosecution over alleged false statements to Congress.
Fauci has repeatedly denied Paul's allegations and said he did not do anything wrong.

Paul, the top Republican on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, subpoenaed Fauci to testify Wednesday about the origins of COVID-19 after he declined to appear voluntarily.

Fauci repeatedly pleaded the Fifth, arguing Paul had an "obsession" with seeking his arrest and released more than 1,000 pages of his "personal diary" over the weekend in an effort to embarrass and intimidate him, according to his opening statement.
Fauci's refusal to answer any questions came as a surprise to Paul and his staff, who believed the ex-COVID-19 czar would not invoke his Fifth Amendment rights.
So confident, a source familiar told Fox News Digital, that several questions were prepared ahead of time, and members of the committee were told to come prepared for Fauci’s rebuttals.

Some Republicans on the panel have argued that the sweeping pardon former President Joe Biden granted Fauci would not shield him from contempt sanctions because any alleged misconduct would have occurred after the pardon was issued.

The unprecedented pardon covers any federal offenses the ex-COVID-19 czar may have committed between Jan. 1, 2014, and Jan. 20, 2025 regarding his leadership over the NIAID and helming the nation’s COVID-19 response, among other government service.

"You don't have any rights under the Fifth Amendment because you've been pardoned," Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said during the fiery hearing. "You know that. Your lawyer is sitting behind you now, shifting nervously in their chairs. They know it. This isn't about the Constitution. This isn’t about the law."
"This is about contempt, contempt for this body and contempt for the American people," he continued.
Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he was not surprised Fauci exercised his Fifth Amendment rights.

"I certainly understand why, on the advice of counsel, you're not answering any questions," Johnson said during the hearing. "Because I think it'd be almost impossible for you to answer the questions truthfully. Without really demonstrating what you did, your culpability."
After Fauci's lawyer, David Schertler, a prominent criminal defense attorney, attempted to speak without being recognized, Paul directed Capitol Police to eject him from the hearing room.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday that he will seek contempt charges against Dr. Anthony Fauci, the former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Director.  (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
READ THE DIARIES: DOCUMENTS UNVEIL FAUCI'S THOUGHTS ON THE LAB-LEAK DEBATE, MASK DOUBTS AND TESTING FAILURES
The planned committee vote is likely to be along party lines as several Democrats on the panel came to Fauci’s defense on Wednesday.

If approved by the committee, the contempt resolution would head to the full Senate, where Democrats could filibuster it. The resolution would need 60 votes to advance, requiring at least some Democratic support.
Democrats on the panel accused Paul of leading a partisan oversight investigation that cut them out, including failing to share documents before Republicans publicly released them.

"This hearing appears to be a culmination of months of biased and selected efforts by the majority, under the guise of a committee investigation, to basically legitimize a predetermined conclusion that was reached years ago," Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., said during his opening statement.

The lead Democrat also accused Paul of "relitigating the past" instead of holding the annual threats hearing or an oversight hearing on the Department of Homeland Security's budget request for the upcoming fiscal year.
Paul fired back that Peters’ claim that the committee blocked the minority from accessing records is "categorically false" and claimed the probe was the "most transparent investigation" in history.
"We actually created a website, and we put all of the information on the website. It continues to operate," Paul added. "The reason it hasn't been accessed is no Democrat ever signed up for it."

title: Soft exosuit helps people walk without bulky motors
summary: A 4.2-pound soft exosuit using artificial muscles instead of motors cut walking energy use by nearly 14% in treadmill tests with six adults.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Walking through an airport or around a large store can take more energy as we get older. Researchers in China are now testing a soft robotic suit that could someday help your legs do some of that work.

The experimental soft exosuit assists the hips using thin artificial muscles instead of conventional motors and gearboxes. The research, published in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances, describes a 4.2-pound prototype that fits around the waist and thighs like a lightweight harness.
In a small treadmill test, six healthy adults used an average of 13.9% less energy while the powered assistance was active. Sensors also showed that their leg muscles worked less.
So, how does the soft exosuit actually work, and what still needs to improve before you could ever wear one?
SELF-DRESSING CLOTHES COULD HELP OLDER ADULTS
The experimental soft exosuit fits around the waist and thighs, moving with the wearer like a lightweight harness. (Ziqi Zhang, Wei Yu et al./Science Advances)

How the soft exosuit helps people walk

Many robotic exoskeletons rely on rigid motors to move a person’s joints. Others use compressed air, which requires pumps, valves and an air tank. Those components can make an exoskeleton heavy or noisy. They can also restrict how naturally your body moves.

The new soft exosuit takes a different approach. It uses flexible muscle-like fibers positioned near each hip. As you walk, the fibers pull at the right point in your stride to help move your leg forward. Straps transfer that pulling force from the artificial muscles to the wearer’s hips and thighs. The flexible design allows the suit to move with the body rather than enclosing the legs inside a rigid frame. "Motor-free" refers to the lack of traditional motors and gearboxes. The suit still uses a compact battery pack and electrical power system to activate its artificial muscles.
Artificial muscles replace heavy motors

The artificial muscles use a rubber-like material called a dielectric elastomer. The material changes shape when exposed to an electric field. Researchers have studied dielectric elastomers for years. However, earlier designs lacked the force needed to help move a human leg. Many were also too bulky for a comfortable wearable device.

Wei Yu and his colleagues at Hebei University of Technology changed the molecular structure of the material to improve its performance. They then rolled thin layers into long fibers. Next, the team grouped several fibers into bundles. The arrangement works somewhat like human muscle, where many smaller fibers pull together to create greater force.

The researchers also created modular connectors that allow them to add more fibers when an application requires additional pulling power. According to Hebei University of Technology, the actuators completed more than 100,000 cycles during laboratory testing. Longer studies will need to show how well the materials hold up during daily wear.
COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?
Researchers say the technology could eventually support older adults and people recovering from injuries, but more safety testing is needed. (iStock)
Soft exosuit trial cut walking energy use by 13.9%

The researchers tested the soft exosuit on six healthy volunteers. Each participant walked on a treadmill under several conditions. They walked without the suit. They also wore it with the artificial muscles turned off. During another round, the electrical assistance actively supported their hips.

A metabolic testing system measured how much oxygen each person used. Sensors attached to their legs also tracked muscle activity. When the assistance was active, the volunteers used an average of 13.9% less energy than they used while walking without the suit. Lower muscle activity also suggested that their legs needed less effort to complete each step.

That reduction could feel meaningful during a long walk. However, this study involved a controlled treadmill setting and a very small group. The volunteers were also healthy adults. Researchers still need dedicated studies involving older people and those with mobility challenges.
Why a soft exosuit could help older adults

A wearable device that reduces walking effort could help people stay active longer as their leg strength changes. Think about walking through a large grocery store or spending the day with family. A lightweight suit that takes some strain away from your hips could make those outings feel more manageable.

The design may also feel less intimidating than a rigid robotic frame. Its artificial muscles resemble cords built into clothing, while the supporting straps fit close to the body. People recovering from surgery could also benefit from this type of assistance one day.However, future clinical trials will need to determine who can use the suit safely and how much support each person needs. Balance presents another important consideration. The current study focused on the energy required for walking rather than fall prevention or stability.
What the soft exosuit still needs before everyday use

The current prototype remains an early research system. Battery life limits how long the suit can provide assistance. The researchers want future versions to operate longer without adding much weight.

The control system also needs to respond automatically when a person speeds up or slows down. Walking across grass or climbing a slope would create additional challenges. Voltage presents another hurdle. Dielectric elastomer actuators often require more than 1,000 volts. The current stays very low, but any wearable consumer product would need strong insulation and extensive safety testing.

Researchers will also need to study how the fibers respond to sweat and changing temperatures. Repeated bending during everyday activities could affect long-term performance as well. No consumer price or release date has been announced.
FDA TO REVIEW 7 POPULAR PEPTIDES TOUTED FOR WEIGHT LOSS, HEALING AND LONGEVITY
A lightweight robotic suit reduced walking energy use by an average of 13.9% in a small treadmill study involving six healthy adults. (Yurii Rylchuk / Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)
What this means to you

You will not be buying this soft exosuit anytime soon, but the research shows where mobility support could be headed. A lighter system that moves with your body could feel far more natural than today's bulky powered exoskeletons.
The nearly 14% drop in walking energy use is encouraging. Still, the test involved only six healthy adults on a treadmill, so we need much more evidence about comfort, safety and real-world use.

The next big step is testing the suit with older adults and people who already have trouble walking. That is where we will learn whether these artificial muscles can truly help people stay active and independent. For now, anyone noticing changes in mobility should talk with a doctor or physical therapist about the support that makes sense today.
Kurt’s key takeaways

What grabs me here is how much walking support the researchers created without loading someone down with bulky motors. A 4.2-pound suit that cut energy use by nearly 14% is worth watching. Still, this was a very small lab test with only six healthy adults. The battery needs to last longer, and the high-voltage system will need serious safety testing. The bigger test comes next. I want to see how this soft exosuit performs with older adults on real sidewalks and over longer periods before we call it a true mobility breakthrough.

title: Wearable patch vibrates when danger is nearby
summary: NC State researchers built a solar-powered wearable patch with six sensors that vibrates against your skin using distinct haptic alerts for each hazard.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Your phone can warn you about bad weather or heavy traffic. However, some dangers cannot wait for you to notice a notification. A hazardous gas may already surround you. Contaminated water may look perfectly normal. By the time you unlock your phone and check an alert, you could have already spent valuable time near the threat.

Researchers at North Carolina State University have developed a wearable patch that takes the phone out of that warning process. The device detects environmental hazards, then vibrates directly against your skin.
Different vibration patterns tell you which hazard the patch detected. Meanwhile, a related version gives robots their own form of chemical awareness.

Our free CyberGuy Live class "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. SELF-DRESSING CLOTHES COULD HELP OLDER ADULTS

Researchers developed a wearable patch that detects hazardous gases and water contaminants, then warns users with vibrations directly against the skin before they check a phone. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A wearable warning you can feel immediately

The square patch is slightly smaller than a driver's license. That makes it compact enough to attach to clothing or place directly against the skin. Inside, a microcontroller acts as the patch's brain. A small battery powers the system. Six sensors monitor the surrounding environment for potential hazards.

The researchers designed the sensors to detect threats in the air and contaminants in water. Examples include dangerous gases and heavy metals. Once the patch detects a hazard, a tiny actuator creates a vibration against your skin. That physical alert could be harder to overlook than another phone notification.

"If you're coming into contact with a hazardous substance, you need to know as quickly as possible," said Erim Uzunoğlu, the paper's first author and a Ph.D. student at NC State. The research appears in the scientific journal Device.
Why the patch uses vibrations instead of phone alerts

Environmental sensors already exist. Many can send a warning to your smartphone. However, that approach depends on you noticing the alert. Your phone could be in a pocket, buried in a bag or silenced during work.

A physical vibration removes that extra step. The warning reaches your body as soon as the sensor detects a potential threat. Still, the researchers found that adding a small vibrating motor was not enough. The sensation had to feel strong and distinct without becoming uncomfortable.

To solve that problem, they created tiny textured surfaces between the motor and the skin. These surfaces resemble miniature patterns of raised bumps. By changing the size and spacing of the bumps, the team adjusted how each vibration felt. As a result, the alert became easier to notice. The design could prove helpful in loud environments where an audible alarm might disappear into the background.
Different vibration patterns identify each hazard

The patch does not use the same buzzing sensation for every warning. Instead, it produces a separate haptic sequence for each hazard. One pattern might signal a dangerous gas. Another could warn about a contaminant in water.

This creates a small tactile language between the patch and the person wearing it. Therefore, you may understand the type of threat without checking a display. In proof-of-concept testing, the patch successfully detected the targeted substances. It also triggered the appropriate vibration immediately.
However, people would need time to learn what each pattern means. Clear training would become especially important in workplaces where several hazards may be present.
Solar cells help extend the battery life

A wearable safety device offers little protection when its battery dies halfway through the day. To reduce that risk, the researchers placed thin-film photovoltaic cells on the patch's exterior. These cells collect solar energy while someone wears the device.

The solar cells work alongside the internal battery. At the same time, the sensors use relatively little power. During testing, that combination kept the device operating for around 24 hours. That running time could cover a full work shift. However, real-world performance would depend on sunlight, sensor activity and how someone wears the patch.
COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

A new wearable sensor uses distinct vibration patterns to alert users to environmental dangers, while a companion system gives robots the ability to detect chemical hazards. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Researchers give robots a chemical warning system

As the team developed the wearable patch, the researchers began considering another question. Could a robot use the same tactile warning system? That idea led to an electronic skin, also called e-skin.

The robotic version places the sensor patch over a piezoelectric layer. When the patch vibrates, that movement creates an electrical signal. The robot can read the signal and identify the vibration pattern. It can then respond to the detected hazard without waiting for a wireless message.

During testing, researchers placed the e-skin on quadrupedal robots. When the robots detected chemical hazards, they changed direction and followed a safer route. This system could help robots explore locations that may be unsafe for people. It could also let a machine respond when wireless connections become unreliable.
Why the robot e-skin could be important

Most robots rely heavily on cameras and digital instructions to understand their surroundings. Yet a camera cannot always identify a dangerous gas or invisible contaminant. The e-skin gives a robot another way to sense risk. More importantly, it turns the chemical warning into a physical signal within the robot's body.

That direct connection could support faster decisions. The robot would not need to transmit sensor data to a remote computer before responding. For example, a robot could inspect an industrial site while watching for leaks. It could then stop or change direction when it encounters a dangerous substance.
However, this work remains at the proof-of-concept stage. Researchers will need to test the system across harsher conditions before it can support high-risk missions.

Many experimental wearables rely on highly specialized components. Those custom parts can increase costs and slow production. In contrast, the researchers built most of this patch and e-skin with components that are already available. Only a few elements required custom engineering. That could make the technology easier to scale.

The sensor array is also modular. Developers could remove sensors that are unnecessary for a certain environment. They could then add sensors for hazards tied to a specific job or location. A water-quality worker would need a different setup than someone inspecting an area for chemical leaks.
What this means to you

You cannot buy this wearable hazard detection patch yet. Still, the research shows how safety alerts could move beyond screens and speakers. A vibration against your skin may reach you faster than a notification on your phone. That could become especially valuable when every second affects your exposure.

The technology may eventually help people who work near chemicals or inspect questionable water supplies. It could also support emergency teams entering places where the air may be unsafe. However, several questions remain. Researchers must determine how the patch performs after repeated wear and exposure to harsh conditions. They will also need to reduce false alarms and make each vibration easy to recognize. Comfort will play a role too. A safety patch only works when people are willing to wear it throughout the day.
NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL
Scientists at North Carolina State University created a smart patch that could help workers recognize dangerous chemicals through touch instead of smartphone notifications. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

A warning can only protect you when it reaches you in time. This wearable patch brings the alert directly to your skin instead of relying on a phone that you may never check. The separate vibration patterns are especially clever. They could tell you which danger is nearby before you even look at a screen. Meanwhile, the robot e-skin gives machines a physical way to recognize chemical threats and move away from them. That could eventually keep people farther from hazardous areas. The next challenge will be turning a successful laboratory prototype into something durable, comfortable and dependable enough for daily use.

title: What your internet provider, websites and advertisers see
summary: Your internet provider, websites and advertisers can track your browsing activity even without you posting online. Here's how to limit what they see.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson lays out how to limit what health apps used by insurance companies can track about you, the user.
Most people assume that if they are not posting on social media or sharing personal information online, they are staying relatively private. Unfortunately, that isn't how today's internet works.

Every time you browse the web, multiple companies can collect information about you. Your internet provider can monitor certain parts of your online activity, websites can gather data about your visits and advertising companies can use tracking tools to build profiles based on your browsing habits.
The good news? Knowing what others can see is the first step toward protecting your privacy.
AI WEARABLE WATCHES YOU TO PREDICT WHAT YOU NEED
